cards.q: Which structure is the first part of the respiratory zone?
cards.a: The respiratory bronchiole.
options: The respiratory bronchiole
The terminal bronchiole
The segmental bronchus
The trachea
cards.explanation: The respiratory zone begins where alveoli first appear in the airway wall, and that is the respiratory bronchiole, so gas exchange can start there. The terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway, with no alveoli in its wall. The segmental bronchus and the trachea are larger conducting airways that only move air.

cards.q: Across which structure does gas move between air and blood in the lung?
cards.a: The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together.
options: The wall of the terminal bronchiole and its smooth muscle
The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together
The cartilage rings of the bronchi
The pleural membrane covering the lung
cards.explanation: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the respiratory membrane, which is the thin alveolar epithelium plus fused basement membranes plus capillary endothelium, a barrier under one micrometer thick. The terminal bronchiole wall and its smooth muscle are too thick and has no capillary bed dedicated to exchange. Cartilage rings hold airways open, and the pleural membrane sits outside the lung entirely.

cards.q: What is the approximate volume of the anatomic dead space in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 150 mL.
options: About 50 mL
About 500 mL
About 150 mL
About 1200 mL
cards.explanation: The conducting airways hold roughly 150 mL of air, close to 1 mL per pound of ideal body weight, and that air never reaches an exchange surface. About 500 mL is a normal tidal volume, not the dead space inside it. About 50 mL is far too small for the whole airway tree, and 1200 mL is closer to residual volume.

cards.q: Besides gas exchange, which of these is a normal function of the respiratory system?
cards.a: Regulating blood pH by adjusting carbon dioxide removal.
options: Producing red blood cells in the alveolar wall
Absorbing nutrients from inspired air
Storing calcium for release during exercise
Regulating blood pH by adjusting carbon dioxide removal
cards.explanation: Because CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, changing how much CO2 the lungs blow off changes blood H+ directly, which makes ventilation one of the two main pH control systems. Red blood cells are made in bone marrow, not in alveoli. Nutrients are absorbed in the gut, and calcium storage belongs to bone.

cards.q: Which airway is the last structure of the conducting zone?
cards.a: The terminal bronchiole.
options: The alveolar duct
The terminal bronchiole
The respiratory bronchiole
The alveolar sac
cards.explanation: The terminal bronchiole is the smallest airway with no alveoli in its wall, so it is the last place that only conducts air. Respiratory bronchioles already carry scattered alveoli and belong to the respiratory zone. Alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs are further downstream and are almost entirely exchange surface.

cards.q: Which cell type forms most of the alveolar surface where gas diffuses?
cards.a: The type I alveolar cell.
options: The alveolar macrophage
The type II alveolar cell
The type I alveolar cell
The ciliated columnar cell
cards.explanation: Type I alveolar cells are extremely flat simple squamous cells, and that thinness is exactly what makes the diffusion distance short enough for rapid gas exchange. Type II cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant, covering only a small fraction of the surface. Macrophages patrol the alveolus for debris, and ciliated columnar cells line conducting airways, not alveoli.

cards.q: What structural feature of conducting zone airways is absent from alveoli?
cards.a: Cartilage or smooth muscle in the wall.
options: A layer of surfactant on the inner surface
A blood supply from pulmonary capillaries
A moist inner surface
Cartilage or smooth muscle in the wall
cards.explanation: Conducting airways need cartilage and smooth muscle to stay open and to change their diameter, while the alveolar wall is a single squamous layer with no such support, which is what keeps the diffusion barrier thin. Surfactant is found in alveoli, not in conducting airways. Both zones are moist, and the alveolus is the site with the densest capillary supply.

cards.q: What does the conducting zone do to inspired air before it reaches the alveoli?
cards.a: Warms it, humidifies it, and filters out particles.
options: Warms it, humidifies it, and filters out particles
Cools it and removes water vapor from it
Adds oxygen to it from bronchial capillaries
Removes carbon dioxide from it before exchange
cards.explanation: Mucus and the rich submucosal blood supply bring air to body temperature and full saturation with water vapor, and the mucociliary escalator traps particles, so the alveoli receive clean conditioned air. Cooling and drying is the opposite of what happens. Oxygen is not added along the way, and carbon dioxide is removed at the alveolus, not in the conducting airways.

cards.q: A person breathes cold dry air at 5 C. What is the condition of that air by the time it reaches the alveoli?
cards.a: Warmed to about 37 C and fully saturated with water vapor.
options: Still near 5 C but fully saturated with water vapor
Warmed to about 37 C and fully saturated with water vapor
Warmed to about 37 C but still dry
Unchanged in temperature and in water content
cards.explanation: The conducting zone is built to condition air, so by the carina and certainly by the alveolus the air is at body temperature and 100 percent humidified, which protects the delicate exchange surface. Air that stayed at 5 C would injure the alveoli and would also be unable to hold much water. Warm but dry air would dehydrate the surface, and truly unchanged air would do both kinds of damage.

cards.q: Tidal volume is 500 mL and anatomic dead space is 150 mL. How much of one breath actually reaches the respiratory zone?
options: 150 mL
500 mL
650 mL
350 mL
cards.explanation: Fresh air reaching exchange surface is tidal volume minus dead space, so 500 minus 150 gives 350 mL per breath. The 150 mL figure is the part that stays in the conducting airways and never exchanges. The full 500 mL ignores dead space entirely, and 650 mL adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

cards.q: A tracheostomy tube bypasses the nose, mouth, and pharynx. What is the immediate effect on the anatomic dead space?
cards.a: It decreases, because part of the conducting zone is bypassed.
options: It decreases, because part of the conducting zone is bypassed
It increases, because a new airway is added in series
It is unchanged, because dead space is fixed by lung size
It falls to zero, because air enters the trachea directly
cards.explanation: Anatomic dead space is the volume of all conducting airways, so removing the upper airway from the path takes roughly half of it away. Adding tubing outside the body would increase dead space, but a tracheostomy shortens the path rather than lengthening it. Dead space is not fixed, and it cannot reach zero because the trachea and bronchi still conduct air.

cards.q: Which change would most directly slow oxygen diffusion into the blood?
cards.a: Thickening of the alveolar and capillary walls.
options: Loss of cartilage from a large bronchus
Thickening of the alveolar and capillary walls
Increased mucus production in the trachea
Weakness of the external intercostal muscles
cards.explanation: Diffusion rate falls as the barrier gets thicker, so any process that adds tissue between alveolar air and capillary blood directly slows gas transfer. Loss of bronchial cartilage and extra tracheal mucus both affect conduction of air, not the exchange barrier itself. Weak intercostals reduce how much air arrives but do not change how fast gas crosses the membrane.

cards.q: A mucus plug completely blocks one terminal bronchiole. What happens to the alveoli downstream of the plug?
cards.a: They stop being ventilated but remain perfused.
options: They stop being perfused but remain ventilated
They continue to exchange gas normally
They stop being ventilated but remain perfused
They immediately fill with fluid from the capillaries
cards.explanation: A terminal bronchiole is the sole air supply to its cluster of alveoli, so blocking it cuts off ventilation while pulmonary capillary blood keeps flowing past, creating blood that leaves the lung without picking up oxygen. Perfusion is set by the pulmonary arteries, not by the airway. Normal exchange is impossible without fresh air, and capillary fluid does not pour into a blocked alveolus.

cards.q: Why does the respiratory zone have a total surface area of roughly 70 square meters?
cards.a: Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area.
options: It provides room to store extra oxygen between breaths
It slows airflow so that air can be warmed
It increases the pressure of gas in the alveoli
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area
cards.explanation: Fick's law makes the amount of gas crossing a membrane proportional to the area available, so hundreds of millions of small alveoli move far more oxygen per second than a few large sacs would. Oxygen is not stored in air spaces in any useful quantity. Warming happens in the conducting zone, and surface area does not change alveolar gas pressure.

cards.q: A patient hypoventilates for several minutes. What happens to arterial pH?
cards.a: It falls, because retained carbon dioxide generates H+.
options: It falls, because retained carbon dioxide generates H+
It rises, because retained carbon dioxide generates HCO3-
It rises, because less oxygen is delivered to tissues
It does not change, because the kidneys fix it within minutes
cards.explanation: CO2 that is not blown off combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates to H+ and HCO3-, so a rising PCO2 always drives pH down. The reaction does yield HCO3-, but it yields H+ at the same time, and it is the H+ that sets pH. Reduced oxygen delivery causes lactate production, which would also lower pH, and renal compensation takes days rather than minutes.

cards.q: A long term smoker has paralyzed airway cilia. Trace the consequence for the conducting zone and for gas exchange.
cards.a: Mucus and trapped particles accumulate in the airways, narrowing them and raising infection risk.
options: Surfactant production falls, so alveoli collapse at the end of every expiration
Mucus and trapped particles accumulate in the airways, narrowing them and raising infection risk
The alveolar membrane thins, so gas exchange temporarily improves
Anatomic dead space falls, so alveolar ventilation rises
cards.explanation: The mucociliary escalator normally sweeps trapped debris upward to be swallowed, so losing ciliary motion leaves mucus sitting in the conducting airways, which narrows the lumen and gives bacteria a place to grow. Surfactant comes from type II alveolar cells and is not made by ciliated cells. The alveolar membrane thickens rather than thins in chronic injury, and a mucus filled airway does not reduce dead space in any helpful way.

cards.q: A disease destroys alveolar walls but leaves every conducting airway wide open. Predict the effect on airflow into the lung and on arterial PO2.
cards.a: Airflow into the lung is preserved but arterial PO2 falls.
options: Both airflow and arterial PO2 are preserved
Airflow into the lung falls but arterial PO2 is preserved
Airflow into the lung is preserved but arterial PO2 falls
Both airflow and arterial PO2 fall in proportion
cards.explanation: The two zones do different jobs, so intact conducting airways still deliver air normally while destroyed alveoli remove the surface where oxygen crosses into blood, and arterial PO2 drops. Saying both are preserved ignores the lost exchange area. Saying airflow falls confuses the conducting zone with the respiratory zone, and a proportional fall in both would require damage to airways as well.

cards.q: A patient shifts from breathing 500 mL twelve times a minute to breathing 250 mL twenty four times a minute. Minute ventilation is unchanged. Why does gas exchange worsen?
cards.a: A larger fraction of each small breath stays in the fixed 150 mL dead space.
options: A larger fraction of each small breath stays in the fixed 150 mL dead space
The dead space volume doubles when breathing frequency doubles
Faster breathing shortens the time available for diffusion across the membrane
Smaller breaths reduce the surface area of the alveoli by half
cards.explanation: Dead space is an anatomic volume that does not shrink with the breath, so a 250 mL breath wastes 150 mL and delivers only 100 mL of fresh air, while a 500 mL breath delivers 350 mL. Dead space does not change with rate, since the airways are the same size. Diffusion across the membrane is complete in about a third of the capillary transit time, so it is not the limiting step here, and alveolar surface area does not change with tidal volume.

cards.q: An inhaled particle 15 micrometers across and one 0.5 micrometers across enter the airway together. Where does each most likely end up?
cards.a: The large particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the small one reaches the alveoli.
options: Both are trapped in the nasal mucosa before reaching the trachea
The small particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the large one reaches the alveoli
Both reach the alveoli because airflow is fast in the bronchi
The large particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the small one reaches the alveoli
cards.explanation: Large particles have too much inertia to follow the sharp turns of the nose and pharynx, so they strike mucus and are cleared, while particles under about one micrometer travel with the airstream all the way to the respiratory zone where only macrophages can remove them. Reversing the two ignores how inertial impaction works. Not everything is trapped in the nose, and airflow velocity actually falls sharply in the small airways because total cross sectional area is so large.

cards.q: What does Boyle's law state about a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature?
cards.a: Pressure varies inversely with volume.
options: Pressure varies inversely with volume
Pressure varies directly with volume
Volume varies inversely with temperature
Pressure is independent of container volume
cards.explanation: Boyle's law says P times V is constant, so squeezing a gas into a smaller space raises its pressure and letting it expand lowers its pressure, which is exactly how the thorax moves air. A direct relationship would mean a bigger chest raises alveolar pressure, which would make inspiration impossible. Volume and temperature are related by Charles's law, and pressure certainly does depend on container volume.

cards.q: What is alveolar pressure at the end of a quiet expiration, before the next breath begins?
cards.a: Equal to atmospheric pressure, or 0 mmHg relative.
options: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric pressure, or negative 4 mmHg
Equal to atmospheric pressure, or 0 mmHg relative
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric pressure, or positive 1 mmHg
About 1 mmHg below atmospheric pressure, or negative 1 mmHg
cards.explanation: Between breaths the airway is open and no air is moving, and airflow stops precisely when the pressure difference is zero, so alveolar pressure has equalized with atmospheric. The value 4 mmHg below atmospheric is intrapleural pressure, not alveolar. The values 1 mmHg above and 1 mmHg below atmospheric occur during expiration and inspiration respectively, when air is actually flowing.

cards.q: What is alveolar pressure during quiet inspiration?
cards.a: About 1 mmHg below atmospheric.
options: About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
About 10 mmHg below atmospheric
About 1 mmHg below atmospheric
Exactly equal to atmospheric
cards.explanation: Thoracic expansion drops alveolar pressure only about 1 mmHg below atmospheric, and that small gradient is enough to move 500 mL of air because airway resistance is low. A pressure above atmospheric would push air out, which is expiration. Ten mmHg below is far larger than a quiet breath requires, and an equal pressure would produce no flow at all.

cards.q: What is alveolar pressure during quiet expiration?
cards.a: About 1 mmHg above atmospheric.
options: About 1 mmHg below atmospheric
About 4 mmHg below atmospheric
About 30 mmHg above atmospheric
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
cards.explanation: As the lung recoils, its volume falls, so by Boyle's law alveolar pressure rises just above atmospheric and air flows out. A pressure below atmospheric would draw air in. The negative 4 mmHg value belongs to the intrapleural space, and pressures near 30 mmHg above atmospheric occur only during forced expiration such as a cough.

cards.q: Which muscle does most of the work of quiet inspiration?
cards.a: The diaphragm.
options: The diaphragm
The rectus abdominis
The internal intercostals
The sternocleidomastoid
cards.explanation: Diaphragm contraction accounts for roughly two thirds of the volume change in a quiet breath, because flattening the dome lengthens the thoracic cavity from top to bottom. The rectus abdominis and internal intercostals are expiratory muscles used during forced breathing. The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory inspiratory muscle recruited only when breathing becomes labored.

cards.q: What drives quiet expiration in a healthy person at rest?
cards.a: Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.
options: Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
Contraction of the abdominal muscles
Relaxation of airway smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Inspiration stretches elastic tissue, and when the inspiratory muscles relax that stored energy pulls the lung back down in volume with no muscular work required. Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles do drive expiration, but only during forced expiration such as exercise or coughing. Airway smooth muscle tone changes resistance, not the volume change that empties the lung.

cards.q: What determines the direction of airflow between the atmosphere and the alveoli?
cards.a: The pressure difference between atmospheric air and alveolar air.
options: The oxygen concentration difference between air and alveoli
The difference between intrapleural and atmospheric pressure
The pressure difference between atmospheric air and alveolar air
The compliance of the chest wall alone
cards.explanation: Bulk flow follows a total pressure gradient, so air moves toward whichever side has the lower pressure, and the relevant two points are the mouth and the alveolus. Oxygen concentration gradients drive diffusion across the membrane, not bulk flow through airways. Intrapleural pressure matters for keeping the lung inflated, and compliance affects how much pressure is needed rather than which way air goes.

cards.q: What happens to thoracic cavity volume when the diaphragm contracts?
cards.a: It increases as the dome flattens and moves downward.
options: It decreases as the dome flattens and moves downward
It stays the same while the ribs move outward
It decreases as the dome rises into the thorax
It increases as the dome flattens and moves downward
cards.explanation: A relaxed diaphragm bulges upward into the thorax, so contraction pulls it flat and down, adding vertical height to the cavity and increasing its volume. Volume cannot decrease while the floor of the cavity descends. The dome rising is what happens during expiration when the diaphragm relaxes.

cards.q: The diaphragm contracts and thoracic volume increases. What happens to alveolar pressure and why?
cards.a: It falls, because the same amount of gas now occupies a larger volume.
options: It rises, because the lungs are stretched outward by the expanding chest wall
It falls, because the same amount of gas now occupies a larger volume
It stays constant, because air enters immediately
It falls, because oxygen is consumed by the alveolar cells
cards.explanation: Boyle's law applies directly, so expanding the alveoli spreads the same gas molecules over more space and pressure drops below atmospheric, which is what pulls air in. Stretching a gas container outward lowers pressure rather than raising it. Air entry follows the pressure drop rather than preventing it, and alveolar oxygen consumption is far too slow to explain a change within one breath.

cards.q: At the exact instant airflow stops at the end of inspiration, what is alveolar pressure?
cards.a: Equal to atmospheric pressure.
options: Below atmospheric pressure
Above atmospheric pressure
Equal to atmospheric pressure
Equal to intrapleural pressure
cards.explanation: Airflow is driven by a pressure difference, so flow reaches zero exactly when that difference reaches zero, which means alveolar pressure has climbed back to atmospheric as air filled the lung. A pressure still below atmospheric would keep pulling air in. A pressure above atmospheric would start expiration, and alveolar pressure never equals the much lower intrapleural pressure in a lung that is still inflated.

cards.q: How do the external intercostal muscles contribute to inspiration?
cards.a: They lift the ribs upward and outward, widening the thorax.
options: They lift the ribs upward and outward, widening the thorax
They pull the ribs downward and inward, narrowing the thorax
They pull the diaphragm downward from above
They compress the abdominal contents against the diaphragm
cards.explanation: Their fibers run downward and forward, so contraction swings each rib up and out in a bucket handle motion that increases the side to side and front to back dimensions of the chest. Pulling ribs down and in is the action of the internal intercostals during forced expiration. The intercostals do not attach to the diaphragm, and abdominal compression pushes the diaphragm up, which empties the lung.

cards.q: Which muscles are recruited during forced expiration?
cards.a: The abdominal muscles and the internal intercostals.
options: The diaphragm and the external intercostals
The abdominal muscles and the internal intercostals
The scalenes and the sternocleidomastoid
The diaphragm and the abdominal muscles together
cards.explanation: Abdominal contraction drives the viscera and the diaphragm upward while internal intercostals pull the ribs down, and together they shrink the thorax faster than recoil alone could. The diaphragm and external intercostals are the inspiratory pair. Scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory inspiratory muscles, and the diaphragm never helps empty the lung because its contraction always enlarges the cavity.

cards.q: Atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg and alveolar pressure is 759 mmHg. Which way is air moving?
cards.a: Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower.
options: Out of the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower
No air moves, because the difference is too small
Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower
Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is higher
cards.explanation: Gas flows from higher to lower pressure, so a 1 mmHg deficit inside the alveolus pulls air inward, which is precisely the gradient of a normal quiet inspiration. Air would leave the lung only if alveolar pressure exceeded atmospheric. A 1 mmHg difference is small but entirely sufficient because airway resistance is low, and describing 759 as higher than 760 misreads the numbers.

cards.q: A sealed 2.0 L container of gas at 760 mmHg is compressed to 1.0 L at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
cards.a: 1520 mmHg.
options: 380 mmHg
760 mmHg
1140 mmHg
1520 mmHg
cards.explanation: Boyle's law gives P1V1 equal to P2V2, so 760 times 2.0 divided by 1.0 equals 1520 mmHg, a doubling of pressure for a halving of volume. The value 380 mmHg comes from dividing instead of multiplying, which is what would happen if the container expanded to 4.0 L. Pressure cannot stay at 760 when volume changes, and 1140 mmHg does not satisfy the equation.

cards.q: Which change would increase the pressure gradient that drives air into the lungs during inspiration?
cards.a: A stronger diaphragm contraction that expands the thorax further.
options: A stronger diaphragm contraction that expands the thorax further
A slower relaxation of the abdominal muscles
An increase in alveolar pressure above atmospheric
A reduction in the elastic recoil of the chest wall during inspiration
cards.explanation: More thoracic expansion means a larger volume increase, which by Boyle's law drops alveolar pressure further below atmospheric and widens the driving gradient. Abdominal relaxation speed does not set the inspiratory gradient. Raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric would reverse flow, and chest wall recoil is not what generates the inspiratory pressure drop.

cards.q: A spinal cord injury silences both phrenic nerves but leaves the intercostal nerves intact. Trace what happens during an attempted quiet breath.
cards.a: The thorax widens only slightly, so alveolar pressure falls less and tidal volume is greatly reduced.
options: The thorax widens only slightly, so alveolar pressure falls less and tidal volume is greatly reduced
The thorax cannot change volume at all, so no air moves in or out
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric, so air is pushed out instead of in
Tidal volume stays completely normal, because the intercostal muscles fully replace the work of the diaphragm
cards.explanation: Losing the diaphragm removes about two thirds of the volume change of a quiet breath, so the intercostals can still widen the ribcage a little and generate a smaller pressure drop, giving a small but nonzero tidal volume. Complete failure would require losing the intercostals as well. Alveolar pressure cannot rise during an attempted inspiration, and the intercostals alone cannot match diaphragmatic descent.

cards.q: A climber breathes at an altitude where atmospheric pressure is 500 mmHg. What must alveolar pressure be for air to flow into the lungs?
cards.a: Slightly below 500 mmHg, for example 499 mmHg.
options: Slightly below 760 mmHg, for example 759 mmHg
Exactly 500 mmHg, since flow depends on volume not pressure
Slightly above 500 mmHg, for example 501 mmHg
Slightly below 500 mmHg, for example 499 mmHg
cards.explanation: What matters is the difference between alveolar and ambient pressure, so at altitude the alveolus must simply be a little below the local 500 mmHg for air to move in. Using 759 mmHg applies sea level numbers to a place where they no longer hold, and that alveolar pressure would push air out at altitude. Equal pressures give zero flow, and a pressure above ambient drives expiration.

cards.q: During a forceful cough, alveolar pressure reaches about 100 mmHg above atmospheric. Compared with quiet expiration, predict the pressure gradient and the airflow rate.
cards.a: Both the gradient and the airflow rate are much larger.
options: The gradient is much larger but airflow rate is unchanged
Both the gradient and the airflow rate are much larger
The gradient is larger but airflow reverses direction
Both the gradient and the airflow rate are smaller
cards.explanation: Forced expiratory muscles compress the thorax hard, so by Boyle's law alveolar pressure climbs far above atmospheric, and since flow equals the pressure difference divided by resistance, flow rises with it, which is what makes a cough able to expel mucus. Airflow cannot stay unchanged when the driving pressure rises a hundredfold. Flow direction is still outward because the alveolus is the high pressure side, and nothing here makes the gradient smaller.

cards.q: A drug completely paralyzes all respiratory muscles while the airway remains open to room air. Predict thoracic volume change, alveolar pressure, and airflow.
cards.a: Volume settles and stops changing, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric, and airflow is zero.
options: Volume rises steadily, alveolar pressure falls, and air flows in continuously
Volume falls steadily, alveolar pressure rises, and air flows out continuously
Volume settles and stops changing, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric, and airflow is zero
Volume is unchanged, alveolar pressure falls steadily, and air continues to flow into the lung
cards.explanation: Without muscle contraction the chest cannot change volume, so after the lung recoils to its resting point there is no further Boyle's law effect, alveolar pressure equilibrates with atmospheric, and bulk flow ceases. Continuous inflow or outflow would require a sustained volume change that no muscle is producing. Alveolar pressure cannot stay below atmospheric while the airway is open and volume is fixed.

cards.q: What is intrapleural pressure in a healthy person at the end of a quiet expiration?
cards.a: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric.
options: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric
Equal to atmospheric
About 4 mmHg above atmospheric
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
cards.explanation: The pleural space sits between two structures pulling away from each other, and that traction holds it at roughly 4 mmHg subatmospheric at rest, with values near negative 6 mmHg at the height of inspiration. A pressure equal to atmospheric means the seal has been lost and the lung collapses. Positive intrapleural pressures are abnormal and occur only with forced expiration or trapped air.

cards.q: How is transpulmonary pressure defined?
cards.a: Alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure.
options: Atmospheric pressure minus alveolar pressure
Alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure
Intrapleural pressure minus atmospheric pressure
Alveolar pressure minus atmospheric pressure
cards.explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is the distending pressure across the lung wall, so it compares the pressure inside the alveolus with the pressure just outside the lung in the pleural space, and it is always positive in an inflated lung. Atmospheric minus alveolar is the gradient that drives airflow, not the one that holds the lung open. The other two subtractions do not describe any pressure across the lung tissue.

cards.q: Which two opposing forces create the subatmospheric intrapleural pressure?
cards.a: Inward elastic recoil of the lung and outward recoil of the chest wall.
options: Inward recoil of the chest wall and outward recoil of the lung
Contraction of the diaphragm and relaxation of the intercostals
Inward elastic recoil of the lung and outward recoil of the chest wall
Surface tension of the alveoli and pressure of the pulmonary capillaries
cards.explanation: The lung always tries to shrink and the chest wall always tries to spring outward, and because the pleural fluid holds them together these opposite pulls stretch the pleural space and lower its pressure. Reversing which structure pulls which way describes a situation that would compress the pleural space and raise its pressure. Muscle activity changes the pressure during a breath but does not create the resting negativity, and capillary pressure plays no role here.

cards.q: What is the main function of the thin layer of pleural fluid?
cards.a: It couples the lung to the chest wall by surface tension while allowing them to slide.
options: It lowers the surface tension inside the alveoli so that they stay open at end expiration
It supplies oxygen to the outer surface of the lung
It cushions the lung against the pressure of the heart
It couples the lung to the chest wall by surface tension while allowing them to slide
cards.explanation: The fluid behaves like water between two glass slides, letting the layers glide during a breath while making them nearly impossible to pull apart, which is how chest wall expansion is transmitted to the lung. Lowering the surface tension inside the alveolus is the job of surfactant, which is a different secretion. Oxygen reaches lung tissue through bronchial and pulmonary circulations, and cushioning is not the physiological point of the coupling.

cards.q: What happens to intrapleural pressure during inspiration?
cards.a: It becomes more negative, falling to about 6 mmHg below atmospheric.
options: It becomes more negative, falling to about 6 mmHg below atmospheric
It becomes less negative, rising toward atmospheric
It becomes positive, rising to about 6 mmHg above atmospheric
It stays fixed at about 4 mmHg below atmospheric
cards.explanation: Chest wall expansion pulls the pleural surfaces further apart and stretches the lung more, so the pressure in that sealed space drops further below atmospheric during every inspiration. Rising toward atmospheric happens during expiration as the lung recoils. Positive intrapleural pressure during inspiration would collapse the lung, and the pressure is not fixed since it cycles with each breath.

cards.q: What is a pneumothorax?
cards.a: Air in the pleural cavity.
options: Fluid in the alveolar air spaces
Air in the pleural cavity
Blood in the pulmonary capillaries
Collapse of a bronchus from outside pressure
cards.explanation: The prefix pneumo means air and thorax names the chest cavity, so a pneumothorax is air that has entered the normally airtight pleural space, destroying the pressure gradient that holds the lung open. Fluid in the alveoli describes pulmonary edema. Blood in the pulmonary capillaries is normal, and external compression of a bronchus is a separate airway problem.

cards.q: What does the term atelectasis mean?
cards.a: Collapse of lung tissue so that alveoli contain no air.
options: Overinflation of alveoli beyond their normal volume
Inflammation of the pleural membranes
Collapse of lung tissue so that alveoli contain no air
Thickening of the alveolar capillary membrane
cards.explanation: Atelectasis is airless collapsed lung, which happens when transpulmonary pressure falls to zero or when an obstructed region absorbs its trapped gas. Overinflation is the opposite problem and is seen in emphysema. Pleural inflammation is pleurisy, and a thickened exchange membrane is a diffusion problem rather than a collapse.

cards.q: Which pressure directly holds the alveoli open against their tendency to recoil?
cards.a: Transpulmonary pressure.
options: Atmospheric pressure
Intrapleural pressure alone
Pulmonary capillary pressure
Transpulmonary pressure
cards.explanation: The lung is distended by the difference between the pressure inside it and the pressure around it, and that difference is transpulmonary pressure, so as long as it stays positive the lung stays inflated. Atmospheric pressure by itself is just a reference point. Intrapleural pressure matters only in comparison with alveolar pressure, and capillary pressure acts on blood vessels rather than on the air spaces.

cards.q: Alveolar pressure is 0 mmHg and intrapleural pressure is 4 mmHg below atmospheric. What is transpulmonary pressure?
cards.a: 4 mmHg.
options: 4 mmHg
0 mmHg
Negative 4 mmHg
8 mmHg
cards.explanation: Subtracting negative 4 from 0 gives positive 4 mmHg, a distending pressure that keeps the lung inflated at the resting volume. A value of 0 would mean no distending force and the lung would collapse. Negative 4 comes from reversing the subtraction, and 8 mmHg would require an intrapleural pressure of negative 8.

cards.q: At the peak of inspiration alveolar pressure is 1 mmHg below atmospheric and intrapleural pressure is 6 mmHg below atmospheric. What is transpulmonary pressure?
cards.a: 5 mmHg.
options: 7 mmHg
5 mmHg
Negative 5 mmHg
1 mmHg
cards.explanation: Negative 1 minus negative 6 equals positive 5 mmHg, larger than the resting value of 4, which is exactly why the lung is more inflated at this moment. Adding the two magnitudes gives 7 and ignores that both numbers are negative. Negative 5 reverses the subtraction, and 1 mmHg is just the alveolar value on its own.

cards.q: A knife wound opens the chest wall into the pleural cavity on one side. What happens to that chest wall immediately?
cards.a: It springs outward, because its own outward recoil is no longer opposed.
options: It collapses inward, following the collapsing lung
It springs outward, because its own outward recoil is no longer opposed
It stays exactly where it was, because ribs are rigid
It moves outward, but only during the next inspiratory effort by the muscles
cards.explanation: The chest wall is normally held in, compressed slightly by the lung pulling inward through the pleural coupling, so breaking the seal lets it expand toward its own larger resting position while the lung recoils away from it. The chest wall and lung move in opposite directions, not together. The ribcage is springy rather than rigid, and the movement is immediate rather than waiting for the next inspiratory effort.

cards.q: Why does a pneumothorax on the right side usually leave the left lung inflated?
cards.a: Each lung sits in its own separate pleural cavity.
options: The left lung is supported by the heart
The left lung has stronger elastic recoil
Each lung sits in its own separate pleural cavity
The mediastinum seals the airways on the left
cards.explanation: The two pleural sacs do not communicate, so air entering one leaves the pressure in the other untouched and that lung keeps its normal transpulmonary pressure. The heart does not hold the lung open. Stronger recoil would make a lung collapse more readily, not less, and the mediastinum does not seal off airways.

cards.q: A large volume of fluid accumulates in one pleural cavity. What is the effect on the lung on that side?
cards.a: The lung is compressed because the fluid raises pleural pressure toward atmospheric.
options: The lung expands because the fluid improves pleural coupling
The lung is compressed because the fluid raises pleural pressure toward atmospheric
The lung is unaffected because fluid cannot transmit pressure
The lung stiffens because the pleural fluid dilutes the surfactant lining the alveoli
cards.explanation: Extra fluid takes up space in the sealed cavity and pushes pleural pressure up, which shrinks transpulmonary pressure and lets the lung recoil to a smaller volume. A thin film couples the layers, but a large collection separates them and pushes them apart. Fluid transmits pressure very effectively, and pleural fluid does not reach the surfactant lining inside the alveoli.

cards.q: What normally prevents the lungs from collapsing to their own resting volume inside the chest?
cards.a: The subatmospheric intrapleural pressure created by the pleural seal.
options: Cartilage rings that hold the alveoli open
Continuous low level contraction of the diaphragm muscle between breaths
The positive pressure of the pulmonary arteries
The subatmospheric intrapleural pressure created by the pleural seal
cards.explanation: Because pleural pressure is lower than alveolar pressure, there is a net outward distending force on the lung at all times, and that is why an excised lung shrinks but an intact one does not. Cartilage supports conducting airways and never reaches alveoli. The diaphragm relaxes between breaths, and pulmonary arterial pressure acts inside vessels rather than distending air spaces.

cards.q: During a maximal forced inspiration against a closed airway, what happens to intrapleural pressure?
cards.a: It becomes far more negative, reaching values such as 20 mmHg below atmospheric.
options: It becomes far more negative, reaching values such as 20 mmHg below atmospheric
It becomes positive, reaching values such as 20 mmHg above atmospheric
It stays near 4 mmHg below atmospheric because the airway is closed
It equalizes with atmospheric because no air can enter
cards.explanation: Powerful inspiratory effort expands the chest wall strongly, and with no air able to enter, the pleural space is stretched much further than in a normal breath, driving its pressure sharply down. Positive values occur with forced expiration against a closed airway, which is the opposite maneuver. The pressure does change even without airflow because the volume of the sealed space changes.

cards.q: A needle punctures the chest wall and air rushes into one pleural cavity. Trace the change in intrapleural pressure, transpulmonary pressure, and lung volume.
cards.a: Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure falls to zero, and the lung collapses.
options: Intrapleural pressure falls further, transpulmonary pressure rises, and the lung overinflates
Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure falls to zero, and the lung collapses
Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure rises, and the lung stays inflated
Intrapleural pressure is unchanged, transpulmonary pressure falls, and the lung partly deflates
cards.explanation: Once the sealed space is open to the outside, its pressure can only equal atmospheric, so alveolar minus intrapleural becomes zero and nothing opposes the lung's elastic recoil. A further fall in pleural pressure would require the space to stay sealed. Transpulmonary pressure cannot rise when the pressure outside the lung goes up, and intrapleural pressure certainly does change once the cavity is open.

cards.q: A chest injury creates a flap that lets air enter the pleural space on inspiration but not leave on expiration. Predict what happens to intrapleural pressure over several breaths and to venous return.
cards.a: Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively positive and venous return falls.
options: Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively more negative and venous return rises
Intrapleural pressure stays near zero and venous return is unchanged
Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively positive and venous return falls
Intrapleural pressure oscillates normally and only the injured lung is affected
cards.explanation: A one way valve traps a little more air with every breath, so pressure in that cavity climbs above atmospheric and pushes on the mediastinum, compressing the great veins so that less blood returns to the heart. More negative pressure would require air to be removed rather than added. Pressure cannot stay at zero when volume keeps increasing in a closed space, and the rising pressure spreads beyond the injured side.

cards.q: After a pneumothorax is treated, a drain removes the trapped air and restores a subatmospheric pleural pressure. Explain in order why the lung reinflates.
cards.a: Pleural pressure falls below alveolar pressure, so transpulmonary pressure turns positive and the lung is distended.
options: Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, which pushes the lung outward until it meets the chest wall again
Pleural pressure falls below alveolar pressure, so transpulmonary pressure turns positive and the lung is distended
Elastic recoil of the lung increases, which pulls the alveoli open from within
Surfactant is redistributed, which raises surface tension and reopens the alveoli
cards.explanation: Reinflation is a pressure story: removing pleural air restores the negative pressure outside the lung, so the inside minus outside difference turns positive and stretches the tissue back open. Alveolar pressure only briefly exceeds atmospheric during expiration and is not what holds the lung open. Elastic recoil always acts to collapse the lung, and raising surface tension would promote collapse rather than reopening.

cards.q: An isolated lung is removed from the chest and an isolated chest wall is studied separately. Predict the resting volume of each compared with their volumes in the intact thorax.
cards.a: The lung is smaller than in the thorax and the chest wall is larger.
options: Both are smaller than in the intact thorax
The lung is larger than in the thorax and the chest wall is smaller
Both are larger than in the intact thorax
The lung is smaller than in the thorax and the chest wall is larger
cards.explanation: In the intact chest each structure is held away from its own resting position, the lung stretched open and the chest wall held in, so freeing them lets the lung shrink and the chest wall spring out. Both shrinking would mean the chest wall recoils inward, which contradicts why pleural pressure is negative. Both enlarging would mean the lung is compressed in the thorax, and reversing the two describes the opposite of the resting forces.

cards.q: What does lung compliance measure?
cards.a: The change in lung volume produced by a given change in distending pressure.
options: The change in lung volume produced by a given change in distending pressure
The change in distending pressure produced by a given change in volume
The speed at which air flows through the conducting airways
The force with which the lung returns to its resting volume
cards.explanation: Compliance is delta V divided by delta P, so it answers how much the lung inflates per unit of pressure applied, which is a measure of stretchability. The reversed ratio is elastance, the stiffness of the tissue. Airflow speed depends on airway resistance rather than tissue stretch, and the force of return to resting volume is elastic recoil.

cards.q: What does elastic recoil of the lung describe?
cards.a: The tendency of the stretched lung to return to its smaller resting volume.
options: The ease with which the lung can be inflated
The tendency of the stretched lung to return to its smaller resting volume
The resistance of the airways to airflow during expiration
The pressure needed to overcome the surface tension of the fluid in the trachea
cards.explanation: Elastic recoil is stored energy in stretched elastin and in the alveolar surface film that pulls the lung back down in volume, and it is what powers quiet expiration. Ease of inflation is compliance, the opposite property. Airway resistance is a separate flow property, and the surface tension that matters acts at the alveolar air liquid interface rather than in the trachea.

cards.q: Which expression correctly gives lung compliance?
cards.a: Change in volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure.
options: Change in transpulmonary pressure divided by change in volume
Change in volume multiplied by change in transpulmonary pressure
Change in volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure
Change in volume divided by change in airflow
cards.explanation: Compliance is volume gained per unit of pressure, written as delta V over delta P, and normal lung values are near 200 mL per cmH2O. Inverting the ratio gives elastance, which rises when compliance falls. Multiplying the two has no physiological meaning, and dividing volume by airflow gives a time, not a stretch property.

cards.q: How are lung compliance and elastic recoil related?
cards.a: They vary inversely, so high compliance goes with low recoil.
options: They vary directly, so high compliance goes with high recoil
They are unrelated properties of lung tissue
They vary directly, so low compliance goes with low recoil
They vary inversely, so high compliance goes with low recoil
cards.explanation: A lung that stretches easily stores little elastic energy, so it also pulls back weakly, which is why the two properties move in opposite directions. A direct relationship would mean the easiest lung to inflate is also the hardest to keep inflated, which is not how elastic tissue behaves. The two are tightly linked rather than independent.

cards.q: What does pulmonary fibrosis do to lung compliance?
cards.a: It decreases compliance.
options: It decreases compliance
It increases compliance
It leaves compliance unchanged
It increases compliance only during expiration
cards.explanation: Fibrosis lays down stiff collagen in the lung interstitium, so a given distending pressure produces a much smaller volume change and the lung becomes hard to inflate. Increased compliance is what happens in emphysema, where elastic tissue is destroyed instead of added. Compliance is not left untouched by scarring, and it does not change direction between phases of the breath.

cards.q: What does pulmonary fibrosis do to elastic recoil?
cards.a: It increases elastic recoil.
options: It abolishes elastic recoil completely
It increases elastic recoil
It decreases elastic recoil
It leaves elastic recoil unchanged
cards.explanation: The stiff scarred lung pulls back harder toward its resting volume, so recoil is high, which is the necessary partner of the low compliance that fibrosis produces. Decreased or abolished recoil describes emphysema, where the elastic fibers themselves are broken down. Because compliance and recoil are inversely linked, recoil cannot stay unchanged while compliance falls.

cards.q: What does emphysema do to lung compliance?
cards.a: It increases compliance.
options: It decreases compliance
It leaves compliance unchanged
It increases compliance
It decreases compliance only during inspiration
cards.explanation: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and their elastin, so the remaining tissue offers little resistance to stretch and a small pressure produces a large volume change, making the lung floppy and easy to inflate. Decreased compliance belongs to fibrosis, where collagen makes the lung stiff. The change is structural and permanent rather than absent or phase dependent.

cards.q: What does emphysema do to elastic recoil?
cards.a: It decreases elastic recoil.
options: It increases elastic recoil
It leaves elastic recoil unchanged
It increases elastic recoil only at high lung volumes
It decreases elastic recoil
cards.explanation: Elastase driven destruction of elastic fibers removes the springs that pull the lung back down, so recoil is lost and the lung tends to stay inflated, which is why these patients trap air. Increased recoil is the fibrosis pattern, paired with low compliance. Recoil cannot remain unchanged when compliance rises, since the two are inversely related.

cards.q: A lung takes in 500 mL when transpulmonary pressure rises by 2 cmH2O. What is its compliance?
cards.a: 250 mL per cmH2O.
options: 250 mL per cmH2O
1000 mL per cmH2O
0.004 mL per cmH2O
100 mL per cmH2O
cards.explanation: Compliance is 500 divided by 2, giving 250 mL per cmH2O, which is at the upper end of the normal adult range near 200. The value 1000 comes from multiplying the two numbers instead of dividing. The tiny value inverts the ratio into elastance units, and 100 would require a 5 cmH2O pressure change.

cards.q: A patient needs a transpulmonary pressure change of 8 cmH2O to move 400 mL of air. What is the compliance and what does it indicate?
cards.a: 50 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung.
options: 3200 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally high and indicates a floppy lung
50 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung
50 mL per cmH2O, which is normal for an adult
200 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung
cards.explanation: Dividing 400 by 8 gives 50 mL per cmH2O, about a quarter of the normal 200, so this lung resists inflation and points toward a restrictive process such as fibrosis. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 3200 and the wrong conclusion. Fifty is well below normal rather than normal, and 200 is the normal figure rather than a low one.

cards.q: Which patient must generate a larger inspiratory pressure to take in a 500 mL breath?
cards.a: The patient with fibrosis, because low compliance resists inflation.
options: The patient with emphysema, because high compliance resists inflation
The patient with fibrosis, because low compliance resists inflation
The patient with emphysema, because low compliance resists inflation
Neither, because compliance affects only expiration
cards.explanation: Low compliance means each milliliter of inflation costs more pressure, so the fibrotic patient does far more inspiratory work for a normal sized breath. High compliance makes inflation easier, not harder, which is why the emphysema patient struggles on the way out rather than the way in. Emphysema raises compliance rather than lowering it, and compliance governs inflation directly.

cards.q: In a patient with emphysema, which phase of quiet breathing becomes difficult and why?
cards.a: Expiration, because the loss of elastic recoil removes the force that empties the lung.
options: Inspiration, because the stiff lung resists stretching
Expiration, because the loss of elastic recoil removes the force that empties the lung
Inspiration, because elastic recoil pulls the lung closed during inflation
Expiration, because the elastic recoil is excessive and pulls the small airways closed
cards.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive and depends entirely on stored elastic energy, so when recoil is destroyed the lung cannot empty on its own and the patient must push air out actively. The emphysematous lung is floppy rather than stiff, so inspiration is easy. Excessive recoil is the fibrosis pattern and would speed emptying rather than slow it.

cards.q: Which two factors together determine lung compliance?
cards.a: The elastic fibers of lung tissue and the surface tension of the alveolar fluid.
options: The diameter of the bronchi and the strength of the diaphragm
The thickness of the pleural fluid and the rate of blood flow
The elastic fibers of lung tissue and the surface tension of the alveolar fluid
The number of type I alveolar cells and the concentration of oxygen in alveolar gas
cards.explanation: Stretching the lung means stretching elastin and collagen and also enlarging the air liquid interface against surface tension, so both must be overcome and both set compliance. Bronchial diameter and muscle strength affect resistance and effort rather than tissue stretch. Pleural fluid volume and pulmonary blood flow do not set the stretchability of the parenchyma, and alveolar oxygen has no direct mechanical effect.

cards.q: A newborn produces almost no surfactant. What is the predicted effect on lung compliance?
cards.a: Compliance falls, because unopposed surface tension resists inflation.
options: Compliance rises, because there is less material lining the alveoli
Compliance is unchanged, because surfactant affects only airway resistance
Compliance rises, because surface tension helps the alveoli expand
Compliance falls, because unopposed surface tension resists inflation
cards.explanation: Surface tension is one of the two forces opposing inflation, so without surfactant to lower it each breath requires far more pressure and the lung behaves as if it were stiff. Removing surfactant does not make the lung easier to inflate, since the lining film is not what resists stretch. Surfactant acts on the alveolar surface rather than on airway caliber, and surface tension always opposes expansion.

cards.q: A pressure volume curve for a diseased lung is much flatter than normal, so each pressure step adds little volume. Which pair of changes does this represent?
cards.a: Low compliance and high elastic recoil.
options: High compliance and low elastic recoil
Low compliance and low elastic recoil
Low compliance and high elastic recoil
High compliance and high elastic recoil
cards.explanation: A flat curve means a small delta V for a given delta P, which is low compliance by definition, and because the two properties are inversely related the recoil force must be high. High compliance would produce a steep curve instead. Low compliance with low recoil, or high compliance with high recoil, would break the inverse relationship between the two.

cards.q: Patient A has a lung compliance of 350 mL per cmH2O and Patient B has 45 mL per cmH2O. Identify the likely disease in each and predict their elastic recoil.
cards.a: A has emphysema with low recoil and B has fibrosis with high recoil.
options: A has fibrosis with high recoil and B has emphysema with low recoil
A has emphysema with low recoil and B has fibrosis with high recoil
A has emphysema with high recoil and B has fibrosis with low recoil
Both have fibrosis, but A is at an earlier stage than B
cards.explanation: Compliance well above the normal 200 means a floppy lung that has lost elastic tissue, which is emphysema, and the same loss means weak recoil, while a compliance of 45 means a stiff scarred lung that pulls back hard. Assigning fibrosis to the high compliance patient reverses the definition of compliance. Pairing emphysema with high recoil ignores that the two properties move in opposite directions.

cards.q: A patient with advanced pulmonary fibrosis is tested. Predict compliance, elastic recoil, and where the extra work of breathing falls.
cards.a: Compliance is low, recoil is high, and the extra work falls on inspiration.
options: Compliance is low, recoil is high, and the extra work falls on inspiration
Compliance is high, recoil is low, and the extra work falls on expiration
Compliance is low, recoil is low, and the extra work falls on expiration
Compliance is high, recoil is high, and the extra work is spread evenly
cards.explanation: Scar tissue makes the lung stiff, so it resists being stretched open and the inspiratory muscles must work much harder, while the strong recoil actually makes emptying easy and even fast. The high compliance and low recoil combination with expiratory difficulty describes emphysema, the opposite disease. Low compliance cannot coexist with low recoil, and neither can high compliance with high recoil.

cards.q: In emphysema, the destruction of elastic tissue also removes the outward pull that surrounding alveoli exert on small airways. Trace the consequence during forced expiration.
cards.a: Small airways lose radial traction and collapse, so air is trapped and residual volume rises.
options: Small airways are held open more firmly, so expiratory flow rises above normal
Small airways lose radial traction and collapse, so air is trapped and residual volume rises
Small airways stay unchanged, so expiratory flow is normal despite the tissue loss
Small airways narrow because of smooth muscle contraction, so residual volume falls instead of rising
cards.explanation: Bronchioles have no cartilage and depend on the surrounding elastic tissue to tether them open, so when that tissue is destroyed the rising pleural pressure of a forced expiration squeezes them shut and gas is trapped behind the closure. Losing tissue cannot hold airways open more firmly. The airways are directly affected by the parenchymal loss, and the problem is loss of tethering rather than smooth muscle contraction, with residual volume rising rather than falling.

cards.q: Two lungs are inflated in the laboratory. Lung X reaches 800 mL at 4 cmH2O of distending pressure, and Lung Y reaches 200 mL at the same pressure. Predict which one empties faster when the pressure is released, and why.
cards.a: Lung Y empties faster, because its lower compliance means stronger elastic recoil.
options: Lung X empties faster, because its higher compliance means stronger elastic recoil
Lung X empties faster, because it holds more air to push out
Lung Y empties faster, because its lower compliance means stronger elastic recoil
Both empty at the same rate, because recoil depends only on airway diameter
cards.explanation: Lung Y gains only 50 mL per cmH2O against Lung X at 200 mL per cmH2O, so Y is the stiff one, and stiffness means it stores more elastic energy and snaps back harder when released. Saying high compliance gives strong recoil reverses the inverse relationship between them. Holding more air does not by itself create a stronger restoring force, and recoil is a property of the tissue rather than of airway diameter.

cards.q: Which cell secretes pulmonary surfactant?
cards.a: The type II alveolar cell.
options: The type I alveolar cell
The alveolar macrophage
The type II alveolar cell
The goblet cell of the bronchial lining
cards.explanation: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal secretory cells that package surfactant into lamellar bodies and release it onto the alveolar surface. Type I cells form the thin diffusion surface but do not secrete. Macrophages clear debris from the alveolus, and goblet cells make mucus in the conducting airways, which is a different secretion entirely.

cards.q: What kind of molecule is the main active component of surfactant?
cards.a: A phospholipid.
options: A steroid
A polysaccharide
A nucleotide
A phospholipid
cards.explanation: Surfactant is mostly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, a phospholipid whose water loving head sits in the fluid film while its water fearing tails point into the air, which is exactly the arrangement that breaks up surface tension. A steroid such as cortisol can stimulate surfactant production but is not surfactant itself. Polysaccharides and nucleotides have no amphipathic structure suited to an air liquid interface.

cards.q: What does the law of Laplace state for a fluid lined sphere such as an alveolus?
cards.a: Collapsing pressure equals twice the surface tension divided by the radius.
options: Collapsing pressure equals twice the surface tension divided by the radius
Collapsing pressure equals twice the radius divided by the surface tension
Collapsing pressure equals surface tension multiplied by the radius
Collapsing pressure equals the radius divided by twice the surface tension
cards.explanation: The relationship P equals 2T over r means that for a fixed surface tension a smaller alveolus generates a larger inward pressure, which is why small alveoli are the ones at risk of collapsing. Putting the radius on top would predict that large alveoli collapse first, the opposite of what happens. The other two forms do not preserve the inverse dependence on radius.

cards.q: What is the direct effect of surfactant on the alveolar fluid lining?
cards.a: It lowers surface tension.
options: It raises surface tension
It lowers surface tension
It thickens the fluid layer
It removes the fluid layer entirely
cards.explanation: Surfactant molecules insert between water molecules at the air liquid interface and weaken their attraction to each other, which is what lowering surface tension means. Raising surface tension would make alveoli harder to keep open. Surfactant does not add bulk fluid, and the thin aqueous film must remain for gases to dissolve and diffuse.

cards.q: What effect does normal surfactant have on lung compliance?
cards.a: It increases compliance.
options: It decreases compliance
It has no effect on compliance
It increases compliance
It increases compliance only during expiration
cards.explanation: Surface tension is one of the two forces the lung must overcome to inflate, so reducing it means less pressure is needed for a given volume change, which is higher compliance. Decreasing compliance is what happens when surfactant is missing. Compliance is affected throughout the breathing cycle rather than in one phase only.

cards.q: When during fetal development does surfactant production usually reach adequate levels?
cards.a: During the third trimester.
options: During the first trimester
During the second trimester
Only after the first breath is taken
During the third trimester
cards.explanation: Type II cells begin secreting surfactant in the later weeks of gestation and reach reliably adequate amounts in the third trimester, which is why prematurity is the main risk factor for surfactant deficiency. The first and second trimesters are too early, as the alveoli themselves are still forming. Production begins before birth rather than being triggered by the first breath.

cards.q: What is the name of the condition caused by surfactant deficiency in a premature newborn?
cards.a: Infant respiratory distress syndrome.
options: Infant respiratory distress syndrome
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
cards.explanation: Infant respiratory distress syndrome is defined by insufficient surfactant, high surface tension, and widespread alveolar collapse in a baby born too early. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis are adult disorders of airway narrowing and interstitial scarring, neither caused by a lack of surfactant. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung injury that can follow prolonged ventilation, so it is a later complication rather than the initial deficiency.

cards.q: What does surface tension at the alveolar air liquid interface tend to do?
cards.a: Pull the alveolar walls inward toward collapse.
options: Push the alveolar walls outward toward expansion
Pull the alveolar walls inward toward collapse
Hold the alveolar walls at a fixed diameter
Increase the rate of oxygen diffusion across the wall
cards.explanation: Water molecules at the surface attract one another strongly and pull the film into the smallest possible area, which for a sphere means shrinking it, so surface tension is always a collapsing force. It cannot push outward, since the attraction between water molecules is inward. It does not fix diameter, and it slows rather than aids gas movement by making the alveolus harder to keep open.

cards.q: Two alveoli have the same surface tension, but one has half the radius of the other. How do their collapsing pressures compare?
cards.a: The smaller alveolus has twice the collapsing pressure.
options: The smaller alveolus has half the collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus has twice the collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus has four times the collapsing pressure
The two have equal collapsing pressures
cards.explanation: Laplace's law puts radius in the denominator, so halving the radius doubles the pressure when surface tension is held constant. Halving the pressure would require the radius to double instead. A fourfold change would happen only if pressure varied with the square of the radius, which it does not, and equal pressures would require equal radii.

cards.q: How does surfactant physically lower surface tension?
cards.a: Its molecules get between water molecules and weaken the hydrogen bonding at the surface.
options: It dissolves the water film completely so that no air liquid interface remains
It adds positive charge that repels the alveolar walls apart
Its molecules get between water molecules and weaken the hydrogen bonding at the surface
It stiffens the alveolar wall so it resists inward pull
cards.explanation: Surface tension comes from water molecules attracting each other, so inserting amphipathic phospholipids between them breaks up that cohesive network and the surface pulls inward much less strongly. The thin fluid film is not dissolved and must remain in place for gases to dissolve and cross. Surfactant does not work by electrostatic repulsion, and it acts on the liquid film rather than on the tissue of the wall.

cards.q: Why do small alveoli not simply empty into larger ones that share the same airway?
cards.a: Surfactant is more concentrated in small alveoli, so it lowers their surface tension more.
options: Small alveoli have thicker walls that resist emptying
Small alveoli are closed off by smooth muscle sphincters
Small alveoli have a higher surface tension of their own, which holds them open against the pressure
Surfactant is more concentrated in small alveoli, so it lowers their surface tension more
cards.explanation: As an alveolus shrinks the same surfactant molecules crowd into a smaller surface, so tension drops further, which offsets the small radius in Laplace's law and equalizes pressures across alveoli of different sizes. Alveolar walls are uniformly thin. There are no sphincters at the alveolar level, and a higher surface tension of their own would promote collapse rather than prevent it.

cards.q: What happens to the work of breathing when surfactant is absent?
cards.a: It increases, because much more pressure is needed to inflate each alveolus.
options: It increases, because much more pressure is needed to inflate each alveolus
It decreases, because the alveoli are already partly collapsed
It is unchanged, because tidal volume is set by the respiratory centers
It decreases, because surface tension helps pull air inward
cards.explanation: With surface tension unopposed, every breath must generate a large transpulmonary pressure just to reopen collapsed alveoli, so muscular work rises sharply and the infant tires. Partly collapsed alveoli make breathing harder, not easier, because they must be reinflated from nothing each time. Work depends on the mechanics of the lung, not only on the neural drive, and surface tension always opposes inflation.

cards.q: A premature infant receives exogenous surfactant into the airway. Predict the effect on surface tension and compliance.
cards.a: Surface tension falls and compliance rises.
options: Surface tension rises and compliance falls
Surface tension falls and compliance falls
Surface tension falls and compliance rises
Surface tension rises and compliance rises
cards.explanation: Replacing the missing phospholipid restores the low tension film, so the lung takes in more volume for the same pressure and becomes easier to inflate. Rising surface tension is what the treatment is designed to prevent. Falling tension cannot lower compliance, since tension is one of the forces opposing inflation, and tension and compliance move in opposite directions.

cards.q: What happens to alveoli at the end of expiration when surfactant is missing?
cards.a: Many collapse completely and must be reopened on the next breath.
options: They stay open but become overinflated
Many collapse completely and must be reopened on the next breath
They fill with surfactant from neighboring alveoli
They remain exactly at their end inspiratory volume
cards.explanation: End expiration is when alveolar radius is smallest, and Laplace's law makes the collapsing pressure highest at exactly that moment, so without surfactant the alveoli close and the next breath must generate a very high opening pressure. Overinflation is the opposite of what high surface tension causes. Surfactant does not migrate between alveoli to rescue them, and volume necessarily falls during expiration.

cards.q: An alveolus with a radius of 100 micrometers shrinks to a radius of 25 micrometers while surface tension stays constant. By what factor does the collapsing pressure change?
cards.a: It increases fourfold.
options: It decreases fourfold
It increases twofold
It increases sixteenfold
It increases fourfold
cards.explanation: Pressure varies as one over the radius, so cutting the radius to one quarter multiplies the pressure by four. A decrease would require the alveolus to enlarge instead. A twofold rise corresponds to halving the radius, and a sixteenfold change would need pressure to depend on radius to the fourth power, which is the rule for airway resistance rather than for surface tension.

cards.q: An infant born at 27 weeks has rapid labored breathing and a stiff lung. Trace the chain from the missing molecule to the clinical picture.
cards.a: Low surfactant raises surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises.
options: Low surfactant raises surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises
Low surfactant lowers surface tension, alveoli overinflate, compliance rises, and the work of breathing rises
Excess surfactant lowers surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises
Low surfactant raises airway resistance, bronchioles constrict, and expiration becomes prolonged
cards.explanation: Every step follows from surface tension being unopposed: the alveoli close at end expiration, the lung becomes hard to inflate, and each breath demands a large pressure from small respiratory muscles. Missing surfactant cannot lower surface tension, since surfactant is what lowers it. There is no excess of surfactant here, and the primary defect is at the alveolar surface rather than in airway smooth muscle.

cards.q: Consider two connected alveoli of unequal size sharing one alveolar duct, with surfactant absent. Predict what happens and explain using Laplace's law.
cards.a: The smaller alveolus empties into the larger one, because its higher collapsing pressure drives air toward the lower pressure sac.
options: Both stay the same size, because they share the same air pressure
The larger alveolus empties into the smaller one, because a bigger radius generates a greater inward collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus empties into the larger one, because its higher collapsing pressure drives air toward the lower pressure sac
Both collapse simultaneously, because collapsing pressure is independent of radius
cards.explanation: With a fixed surface tension the smaller radius produces the greater inward pressure, so gas flows down that pressure gradient into the larger sac and the small one closes, which is exactly what surfactant normally prevents by lowering tension most in the smallest alveoli. Sharing a duct means sharing a connection, not sharing equal pressures. Larger radius means lower pressure, and collapsing pressure clearly does depend on radius.

cards.q: A mother in preterm labor is given a glucocorticoid, which accelerates fetal type II cell maturation. Predict the newborn's surface tension, compliance, and end expiratory alveolar stability.
cards.a: Lower surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration.
options: Higher surface tension, lower compliance, and alveoli that collapse at end expiration
Lower surface tension, lower compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration
Higher surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that collapse at end expiration
Lower surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration
cards.explanation: More mature type II cells make more surfactant, and each downstream effect follows: tension falls, the lung inflates more readily for a given pressure, and the smallest alveoli no longer close at the end of a breath. Higher surface tension describes the untreated premature lung. Falling tension cannot coexist with falling compliance, and stable alveoli cannot coexist with rising tension.

cards.q: In an infant with widespread alveolar collapse from surfactant deficiency, predict what happens to functional residual capacity and to arterial PO2.
cards.a: Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 falls.
options: Functional residual capacity rises and arterial PO2 falls
Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 falls
Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 rises
Both are unchanged because tidal volume is maintained
cards.explanation: Collapsed alveoli hold no gas, so the volume left in the lung at the end of a quiet breath shrinks, and because blood still perfuses those airless regions it leaves the lung without picking up oxygen, dropping arterial PO2. A rising functional residual capacity would require air trapping, which is the emphysema pattern rather than the collapse pattern. Arterial PO2 cannot rise when exchange surface is lost, and maintaining tidal volume does not restore the collapsed regions.

cards.q: What is the main determinant of airway resistance?
cards.a: The radius of the airway.
options: The radius of the airway
The length of the airway
The viscosity of the air
The total number of alveoli
cards.explanation: Resistance depends on radius raised to the fourth power, so even a small change in caliber overwhelms every other variable, which is why bronchodilation and bronchoconstriction matter so much. Airway length and gas viscosity are in the equation but barely change from moment to moment. Alveolar number affects gas exchange surface rather than resistance to flow.

cards.q: According to Poiseuille's relationship, how does resistance depend on the radius of a tube?
cards.a: Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius.
options: Resistance is directly proportional to the radius
Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius
Resistance is inversely proportional to the radius
Resistance is directly proportional to the square of the radius
cards.explanation: The fourth power dependence means halving the radius multiplies resistance by sixteen, which explains why modest airway narrowing produces dramatic changes in the effort of breathing. A simple inverse relationship badly understates the effect. Direct proportionality would mean wider tubes resist flow more, which is backwards.

cards.q: What does sympathetic stimulation do to bronchial smooth muscle?
cards.a: It relaxes the muscle and dilates the airway.
options: It contracts the muscle and narrows the airway
It has no effect, since airways receive only parasympathetic fibers
It relaxes the muscle and dilates the airway
It thickens the airway wall by stimulating mucus glands
cards.explanation: Circulating epinephrine acting on beta 2 receptors relaxes airway smooth muscle, which widens the airways during exercise or stress when more airflow is needed. Contraction and narrowing is the parasympathetic effect. Airways are influenced by both divisions, and sympathetic activity reduces rather than increases airway secretions.

cards.q: What does parasympathetic stimulation through the vagus nerve do to the airways?
cards.a: It causes bronchoconstriction.
options: It causes bronchodilation
It has no effect on airway diameter
It causes bronchodilation and increased mucus clearance
It causes bronchoconstriction
cards.explanation: Acetylcholine released from vagal fibers acts on muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle and contracts it, narrowing the lumen and raising resistance. Bronchodilation is the sympathetic and epinephrine effect. The vagus definitely influences airway caliber, and it increases mucus secretion rather than clearance.

cards.q: Where in the airway tree is total resistance to airflow greatest?
cards.a: In the medium sized bronchi.
options: In the medium sized bronchi
In the terminal bronchioles
In the alveolar ducts
In the respiratory bronchioles
cards.explanation: Although each small bronchiole is narrow, there are so many of them in parallel that their combined cross sectional area is enormous, so most of the resistance sits in the medium bronchi where the airways are still relatively few. Assuming the smallest tube must have the highest resistance ignores how parallel pathways add. Alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles are the most numerous of all and contribute almost nothing to resistance.

cards.q: What effect does histamine released during an allergic reaction have on the airways?
cards.a: It constricts bronchial smooth muscle.
options: It dilates bronchial smooth muscle
It constricts bronchial smooth muscle
It paralyzes the cilia of the airway lining
It destroys elastic fibers in the alveolar wall
cards.explanation: Histamine from mast cells contracts airway smooth muscle and also causes mucosal swelling, both of which narrow the lumen and raise resistance. Dilation would relieve rather than trigger an asthma attack. Ciliary paralysis is caused by tobacco smoke, and elastic fiber destruction is the mechanism of emphysema.

cards.q: Which expression gives airflow through the airways?
cards.a: The pressure gradient divided by the resistance.
options: The pressure gradient multiplied by the resistance
The resistance divided by the pressure gradient
The pressure gradient divided by the resistance
The pressure gradient divided by lung compliance
cards.explanation: Flow equals delta P over R, the same form used for blood flow, so airflow rises with a bigger driving pressure and falls when airways narrow. Multiplying the two would predict that narrower airways carry more air. Dividing resistance by pressure inverts the relationship, and compliance describes tissue stretch rather than opposition to flow.

cards.q: What effect does an increase in carbon dioxide within a region of airway have on the local bronchioles?
cards.a: It dilates them.
options: It constricts them
