It has no local effect
It constricts them only in the presence of histamine
It dilates them
cards.explanation: Local bronchiolar dilation in response to rising CO2 sends more ventilation to regions that are well perfused, which helps match airflow with blood flow. Constriction would send air away from the regions that need it most. The response is a direct local effect and does not require histamine.

cards.q: An airway narrows so that its radius is halved. By what factor does its resistance change?
cards.a: It increases sixteenfold.
options: It increases twofold
It increases fourfold
It increases eightfold
It increases sixteenfold
cards.explanation: Resistance varies as one over the radius to the fourth power, and two raised to the fourth is sixteen, so halving the radius makes the airway sixteen times harder to move air through. A twofold rise assumes a simple inverse relationship. Fourfold assumes a square relationship, and eightfold assumes a cube relationship.

cards.q: During an asthma attack the driving pressure stays the same while airway smooth muscle contracts. What happens to airflow?
cards.a: It falls, because resistance rises.
options: It rises, because resistance rises
It falls, because resistance rises
It is unchanged, because the driving pressure did not change
It falls, because lung compliance falls
cards.explanation: Flow equals pressure divided by resistance, so with the numerator fixed and the denominator climbing steeply, airflow drops, which is why an asthmatic must work harder to move the same volume. Rising resistance can never raise flow. Flow depends on both terms rather than on driving pressure alone, and asthma is an airway caliber problem rather than a compliance problem.

cards.q: Thick mucus partly fills the lumen of a bronchus. How does this raise resistance?
cards.a: It reduces the effective radius available for airflow.
options: It reduces the effective radius available for airflow
It increases the length of the airway
It lowers the compliance of the surrounding alveoli
It raises the viscosity of the inspired air
cards.explanation: Anything occupying the lumen leaves a narrower channel for air, and because resistance depends on radius to the fourth power even a modest layer of mucus has a large effect. Airway length is set by anatomy and is unchanged by secretions. Alveolar compliance is a tissue property, and mucus does not mix into the air to change its viscosity.

cards.q: A patient inhales a beta 2 adrenergic agonist. Predict the effect on airway radius and on airway resistance.
cards.a: Radius increases and resistance falls.
options: Radius decreases and resistance rises
Radius increases and resistance rises
Radius increases and resistance falls
Radius decreases and resistance falls
cards.explanation: Beta 2 receptors on airway smooth muscle relax it when stimulated, so the lumen widens and resistance drops steeply because of the fourth power relationship. Narrowing is what a muscarinic agonist or histamine would produce. Radius and resistance always move in opposite directions, so the two mismatched pairings cannot occur.

cards.q: In a patient with narrowed airways, why is expiration usually more difficult than inspiration?
cards.a: Rising pleural pressure during expiration compresses the airways and narrows them further.
options: The expiratory muscles are inherently weaker than the inspiratory muscles of the chest wall
Rising pleural pressure during expiration compresses the airways and narrows them further
Air is denser during expiration because it is warmer
Airway smooth muscle contracts only during expiration
cards.explanation: During inspiration the falling pleural pressure pulls airways open, while during expiration the pressure around the airways rises and squeezes them, so an already narrowed airway can close off completely. Muscle strength is not the limiting factor here. Expired air is not usefully denser, and smooth muscle tone does not switch on and off with the breathing cycle.

cards.q: Which change would produce the largest increase in airway resistance?
cards.a: A reduction in airway radius from 4 mm to 2 mm.
options: A doubling of the length of the airway
A twofold increase in the viscosity of the gas breathed
A reduction in airway radius from 4 mm to 2 mm
A doubling of the airflow rate through the airway
cards.explanation: Halving the radius multiplies resistance by sixteen, far more than the twofold changes produced by doubling either length or viscosity, both of which appear in the numerator to the first power. Airflow rate is the result of resistance rather than a determinant of it in this relationship.

cards.q: During an asthma attack a patient has bronchial smooth muscle contraction, mucosal swelling, and mucus in the lumen at the same time. Predict airway resistance and the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity.
cards.a: Resistance rises sharply and the ratio falls below normal.
options: Resistance rises sharply and the ratio falls below normal
Resistance rises sharply and the ratio rises above normal
Resistance falls and the ratio falls below normal
Resistance rises sharply but the ratio stays normal
cards.explanation: All three processes shrink the lumen, so resistance climbs steeply, and because a high resistance slows the air leaving the chest, the volume exhaled in the first second drops more than the total exhaled volume, lowering the ratio. A rising ratio is the restrictive pattern seen when the lung is stiff rather than obstructed. Resistance cannot fall when the lumen is narrowed, and an obstructive process does not leave the ratio normal.

cards.q: An airway radius is reduced to half its original value while the patient doubles the driving pressure. What happens to airflow compared with the original?
cards.a: It falls to one eighth of the original.
options: It rises to twice the original
It falls to one half of the original
It falls to one eighth of the original
It stays the same, since the two effects cancel
cards.explanation: Halving the radius raises resistance sixteenfold, and flow equals pressure over resistance, so doubling the pressure gives a flow of two divided by sixteen, which is one eighth. Flow cannot rise when resistance climbs sixteen times faster than the driving pressure. A halving would occur only if resistance had merely quadrupled, and cancellation would require resistance to change by only a factor of two.

cards.q: A healthy person begins vigorous exercise. Trace the effect of sympathetic activation on airway caliber, resistance, and the airflow achievable per unit of effort.
cards.a: Airways dilate, resistance falls, and more air moves for the same driving pressure.
options: Airways constrict, resistance rises, and less air moves for the same driving pressure
Airways dilate, resistance rises, and less air moves for the same driving pressure
Airways dilate, resistance is unchanged, and airflow depends only on muscle strength
Airways dilate, resistance falls, and more air moves for the same driving pressure
cards.explanation: Epinephrine acting on beta 2 receptors relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, and because resistance falls with the fourth power of the widening radius, the same respiratory effort now moves much more air, which is exactly what exercise demands. Constriction during exercise would work against the increased need for ventilation. Dilation must lower resistance, so the pairings with unchanged or rising resistance are internally inconsistent.

cards.q: In emphysema the elastic tissue that tethers small airways open has been destroyed. Predict how airway resistance compares between quiet inspiration and forced expiration in these patients.
cards.a: Resistance is near normal on inspiration but rises sharply on forced expiration as untethered airways collapse.
options: Resistance is equally raised in both phases of the breath because the airway walls are permanently thickened and narrowed
Resistance is near normal on inspiration but rises sharply on forced expiration as untethered airways collapse
Resistance is raised on inspiration but normal on expiration because recoil is strong
Resistance is normal in both phases because emphysema affects only the alveoli
cards.explanation: Falling pleural pressure during inspiration still helps hold airways open, but during forced expiration the surrounding pressure rises and there is no longer any elastic tethering to resist it, so the small airways close and trap air. The airway walls themselves are not thickened in emphysema. Recoil is reduced rather than strong in this disease, and the alveolar destruction has direct consequences for the airways that run through that tissue.

cards.q: What is tidal volume?
cards.a: The volume of air moved in or out during one quiet breath.
options: The volume of air moved in or out during one quiet breath
The maximum volume that can be inhaled after a quiet inspiration
The volume remaining in the lung after a maximal expiration
The total volume the lung can hold at full inflation
cards.explanation: Tidal volume is the ordinary breath at rest, the amount that moves in and out without any extra effort. The extra volume available beyond a quiet inspiration is the inspiratory reserve volume. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume, and full inflation defines total lung capacity.

cards.q: What is the approximate tidal volume of a healthy adult at rest?
cards.a: About 500 mL.
options: About 150 mL
About 500 mL
About 1200 mL
About 3000 mL
cards.explanation: A quiet breath moves roughly 500 mL, of which about 350 mL reaches the alveoli. The 150 mL figure is anatomic dead space, the part of that breath left in the conducting airways. About 1200 mL is close to residual volume, and 3000 mL is closer to the inspiratory reserve volume.

cards.q: What is the inspiratory reserve volume?
cards.a: The extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal inspiration.
options: The air remaining after a maximal expiration
The extra air that can be exhaled beyond a normal tidal expiration
The extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal inspiration
The total air inhaled and exhaled in one minute
cards.explanation: Inspiratory reserve volume is the reserve available on top of a normal breath, roughly 3000 mL in an adult, and it is what a deep breath draws on. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume. The extra air available on expiration is the expiratory reserve volume, and air moved per minute is minute ventilation.

cards.q: What is the expiratory reserve volume?
cards.a: The extra air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration.
options: The air that enters the lung during a maximal inspiration
The air that cannot be exhaled from the lungs no matter how hard a person tries
The air left in the lung at the end of a quiet expiration
The extra air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration
cards.explanation: After a quiet breath out, about 1200 mL can still be forced out with effort, and that reserve is the expiratory reserve volume. Air that cannot be exhaled at all is residual volume. The air present at the end of a quiet expiration is functional residual capacity, which is the expiratory reserve plus the residual volume.

cards.q: What is the residual volume?
cards.a: The air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration.
options: The air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration
The air remaining in the lungs after a quiet expiration
The air remaining in the conducting airways after each breath
The air that can still be inhaled after a quiet inspiration
cards.explanation: Even after blowing out as hard as possible, roughly 1200 mL stays in the lung and keeps the alveoli from collapsing and gas exchange from stopping between breaths. Air present after a quiet expiration is functional residual capacity, a larger number. Air left in the conducting airways is anatomic dead space, and inhalable reserve is the inspiratory reserve volume.

cards.q: Which volumes add together to give vital capacity?
cards.a: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume plus expiratory reserve volume.
options: Tidal volume plus residual volume
Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume plus expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume plus residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume plus the anatomic dead space
cards.explanation: Vital capacity is all the air a person can move voluntarily, which is the ordinary breath plus both reserves, about 4700 mL in an adult. Residual volume cannot be exhaled, so it is never part of vital capacity. Expiratory reserve plus residual volume is functional residual capacity, and adding the anatomic dead space to that gives no meaningful quantity at all.

cards.q: How is total lung capacity defined?
cards.a: Vital capacity plus residual volume.
options: Vital capacity plus tidal volume
Vital capacity minus residual volume
Vital capacity plus residual volume
Inspiratory capacity plus vital capacity
cards.explanation: Total lung capacity is every bit of air the lung holds at full inflation, so it is the volume a person can move plus the volume that always stays behind, about 5900 mL. Adding tidal volume double counts, since tidal volume is already inside vital capacity. Subtracting residual volume would give back vital capacity, and inspiratory capacity is also already contained within vital capacity.

cards.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer?
cards.a: Residual volume.
options: Tidal volume
Expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
cards.explanation: A spirometer records only air that actually moves through it, and residual volume by definition never leaves the lung, so it must be obtained by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography. Tidal volume and both reserve volumes are all exhaled or inhaled through the mouthpiece and are recorded directly.

cards.q: A student has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
cards.explanation: Vital capacity is 500 plus 3000 plus 1200, which is 4700 mL. Leaving out the tidal volume gives 4200. Leaving out the expiratory reserve gives 3500, and 5900 would be total lung capacity once a residual volume of 1200 mL is added.

cards.q: A patient has a vital capacity of 4700 mL and a residual volume of 1200 mL. What is the total lung capacity?
cards.explanation: Total lung capacity is vital capacity plus residual volume, so 4700 plus 1200 gives 5900 mL. Subtracting instead of adding gives 3500. Reporting 4700 ignores the residual volume entirely, and 6100 does not follow from these two numbers.

cards.q: A patient has an expiratory reserve volume of 1200 mL and a residual volume of 1300 mL. What is the functional residual capacity?
options: 100 mL
cards.explanation: Functional residual capacity is the air still in the lung at the end of a quiet expiration, which is the expiratory reserve plus the residual volume, so 1200 plus 1300 gives 2500 mL. Reporting 1300 counts only the residual volume and leaves out the reserve that can still be forced out. Subtracting gives 100, which would leave the lung nearly empty between breaths, and 3000 does not match either number.

cards.q: A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL and an inspiratory reserve volume of 3100 mL. What is the inspiratory capacity?
options: 500 mL
cards.explanation: Inspiratory capacity is the most that can be inhaled starting from the end of a quiet expiration, so it is the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve, giving 3600 mL. Subtracting gives 2600. Reporting either component alone leaves out the other half of the maneuver.

cards.q: A patient has a total lung capacity of 6000 mL and a vital capacity of 4500 mL. What is the residual volume?
cards.explanation: Residual volume is the part of total lung capacity that cannot be exhaled, so it is 6000 minus 4500, which is 1500 mL. Adding the two gives 10500, far beyond any human lung. The value 4500 is the vital capacity itself, and 3000 does not follow from the subtraction.

cards.q: On a spirogram, a subject breathes quietly and then, from the end of a quiet expiration, inhales as deeply as possible. Which value has been measured?
cards.a: Inspiratory capacity.
options: Vital capacity
Inspiratory capacity
Functional residual capacity
Inspiratory reserve volume
cards.explanation: Starting from the resting end expiratory level and filling the lung completely measures inspiratory capacity, which combines the tidal volume and the inspiratory reserve. Vital capacity would require a maximal expiration first. Functional residual capacity is the starting point rather than the excursion, and inspiratory reserve volume is measured from the top of a normal tidal inspiration instead.

cards.q: A subject has a vital capacity of 4800 mL, a tidal volume of 500 mL, and an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL. What is the expiratory reserve volume?
options: 800 mL
cards.explanation: Vital capacity is the sum of the three moveable volumes, so subtracting both 500 and 3000 from 4800 leaves 1300 mL. Subtracting only the inspiratory reserve gives 1800 and forgets that the tidal volume is also part of the sum. The values 2500 and 800 do not satisfy the sum, since adding either to 3500 does not return the measured vital capacity.

cards.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis is tested. Predict what happens to total lung capacity, vital capacity, and residual volume.
cards.a: All three fall below predicted values.
options: Total lung capacity and vital capacity fall while residual volume rises
All three rise above predicted values
All three fall below predicted values
Total lung capacity is unchanged while vital capacity falls and residual volume rises
cards.explanation: Stiff scarred lungs cannot be stretched to a normal size, so every volume shrinks, which is the defining feature of a restrictive pattern. The pattern of falling capacities with a rising residual volume belongs to obstructive disease with air trapping. Rising volumes across the board would require a floppy overinflated lung, which fibrosis is not.

cards.q: A patient with advanced emphysema is tested. Predict the changes in residual volume, functional residual capacity, and vital capacity.
cards.a: Residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls.
options: Residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls
All three fall together because the lung holds less air
Residual volume falls while functional residual capacity and vital capacity rise
Residual volume rises while functional residual capacity and vital capacity are unchanged
cards.explanation: Loss of elastic recoil and collapse of untethered small airways trap gas at the end of every expiration, so residual volume and the resting lung volume both climb, and because the lung is already near full, less of the total remains available to move, so vital capacity falls. A uniform fall in all three is the restrictive picture instead. Residual volume cannot fall when air is being trapped, and functional residual capacity must rise with it, since it contains the residual volume.

cards.q: On a spirogram the pen rises steadily through several quiet breaths, then makes one very large upward excursion followed immediately by one very large downward excursion to the lowest point on the trace. Which measurement does the full excursion represent?
cards.a: Vital capacity.
options: Total lung capacity
Functional residual capacity
Vital capacity
Inspiratory capacity
cards.explanation: A maximal inspiration followed by a maximal expiration moves every milliliter a person can voluntarily move, and that excursion is vital capacity. Total lung capacity cannot be traced this way because it includes residual volume, which never leaves the lung. Functional residual capacity is a resting level rather than an excursion, and inspiratory capacity covers only the upward half of the maneuver.

cards.q: A subject has a total lung capacity of 5800 mL, a functional residual capacity of 2400 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1100 mL. Calculate the residual volume and then the vital capacity.
cards.a: Residual volume 1300 mL and vital capacity 4500 mL.
options: Residual volume 3500 mL and vital capacity 2300 mL
Residual volume 1100 mL and vital capacity 4700 mL
Residual volume 2400 mL and vital capacity 3400 mL
Residual volume 1300 mL and vital capacity 4500 mL
cards.explanation: Functional residual capacity is expiratory reserve plus residual volume, so residual volume is 2400 minus 1100, which is 1300 mL, and vital capacity is total lung capacity minus residual volume, so 5800 minus 1300 gives 4500 mL. Using the total lung capacity minus the functional residual capacity gives 3400, which is inspiratory capacity rather than vital capacity. Treating the expiratory reserve or the functional residual capacity as the residual volume skips the first subtraction.

cards.q: What does forced expiratory volume in one second measure?
cards.a: The volume of air blown out during the first second of a maximal forced expiration.
options: The volume of air blown out during the first second of a maximal forced expiration
The total volume blown out during one maximal forced expiration from full inflation
The volume inhaled during the first second of a maximal inspiration
The volume of air moved during one quiet breath
cards.explanation: This value captures how fast air can leave the chest, which is why it is sensitive to anything that narrows the airways. The total volume blown out over the whole maneuver is forced vital capacity. Measuring inspiration would not test expiratory airflow, and a quiet breath is tidal volume.

cards.q: What does forced vital capacity measure?
cards.a: The total volume exhaled as forcefully and completely as possible after a maximal inspiration.
options: The volume exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration
The total volume exhaled as forcefully and completely as possible after a maximal inspiration
The volume remaining in the lung after a forced expiration
The volume of air exhaled per minute at rest
cards.explanation: Forced vital capacity is the whole amount a person can move out in one maximal effort, so it reflects how much lung is available rather than how quickly it empties. The first second alone is forced expiratory volume in one second. Air left behind is residual volume, and air moved per minute is minute ventilation.

cards.q: What is the approximate normal value for the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in a healthy young adult?
cards.a: About 0.80.
options: About 0.40
About 0.60
About 0.80
About 1.00
cards.explanation: A healthy adult blows out roughly 80 percent of the whole forced vital capacity in the first second, which is why values below about 0.70 are treated as abnormal. Ratios of 0.40 and 0.60 indicate obstruction. A ratio of 1.00 would mean the entire capacity left the lung within one second, which does not occur in normal lungs.

cards.q: What happens to the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in obstructive lung disease?
cards.a: It falls below normal.
options: It rises above normal
It stays exactly normal
It falls below normal
It first rises and then falls
cards.explanation: Narrowed airways slow the exit of air, so the volume delivered in the first second drops much more than the total volume does, and the ratio falls, typically under 0.70. A rising ratio is the restrictive pattern. A normal ratio means airflow is not limited, which is the opposite of obstruction.

cards.q: What happens to the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in restrictive lung disease?
cards.a: It is preserved or even higher than normal.
options: It falls well below 0.70
It falls to about half of normal
It becomes impossible to calculate
It is preserved or even higher than normal
cards.explanation: Restriction shrinks both the volume exhaled in the first second and the total forced vital capacity by similar proportions, and the strong elastic recoil of a stiff lung actually speeds emptying, so the ratio holds up or rises. A ratio below 0.70 defines obstruction rather than restriction. Both values are still measurable, so the ratio can always be calculated.

cards.q: Which disease produces an obstructive spirometry pattern?
cards.a: Asthma.
options: Asthma
Pulmonary fibrosis
Severe scoliosis of the thoracic spine
Muscular dystrophy affecting the diaphragm
cards.explanation: Asthma narrows the airways, which limits how fast air can leave and lowers the ratio, the definition of an obstructive pattern. Pulmonary fibrosis stiffens lung tissue and produces restriction. Scoliosis and diaphragmatic weakness restrict how much the chest can expand, so they also give restrictive patterns rather than obstructive ones.

cards.q: Which disease produces a restrictive spirometry pattern?
cards.a: Pulmonary fibrosis.
options: Chronic bronchitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Emphysema
Asthma
cards.explanation: Fibrosis fills the interstitium with stiff collagen, so the lung cannot expand normally and all volumes fall while airflow stays proportionally well preserved. Chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and asthma all narrow or collapse airways and give obstructive patterns with a reduced ratio.

cards.q: What happens to total lung capacity in restrictive lung disease?
cards.a: It decreases.
options: It increases
It stays normal while only airflow falls
It decreases
It increases early and decreases only in late disease
cards.explanation: Restriction means the lung cannot be filled to a normal size, so total lung capacity is reduced, and this is the measurement that confirms restriction when the ratio is normal. An increased total lung capacity is seen in emphysema because of air trapping. A normal total lung capacity with reduced airflow describes obstruction instead.

cards.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 1.8 L and a forced vital capacity of 3.0 L. Calculate the ratio and classify the pattern.
cards.a: 0.60, an obstructive pattern.
options: 0.60, a restrictive pattern
1.67, an obstructive pattern
0.60, an obstructive pattern
0.60, a normal result
cards.explanation: Dividing 1.8 by 3.0 gives 0.60, well under the 0.70 threshold, so airflow is limited and the pattern is obstructive. Restriction would show a preserved or raised ratio. The value 1.67 comes from inverting the fraction, and 0.60 is clearly below the normal range rather than within it.

cards.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.4 L and a forced vital capacity of 3.0 L, but the predicted forced vital capacity for this patient is 4.8 L. Classify the pattern.
cards.a: Restrictive, because the ratio is 0.80 while the forced vital capacity is far below predicted.
options: Obstructive, because the measured forced vital capacity is far below the predicted value for this patient
Restrictive, because the ratio is 0.80 while the forced vital capacity is far below predicted
Normal, because the ratio of 0.80 is within the normal range
Obstructive, because the ratio of 0.80 is at the lower limit of normal
cards.explanation: The ratio of 2.4 to 3.0 is 0.80, so airflow is not limited, but the lung is only holding about 62 percent of the predicted volume, which is the signature of restriction. A reduced volume alone does not make a result obstructive, since obstruction is defined by the ratio. Calling the result normal ignores that the measured capacity is only about two thirds of predicted.

cards.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 3.2 L and a forced vital capacity of 4.0 L. What is the ratio?
cards.explanation: Dividing 3.2 by 4.0 gives 0.80, a normal ratio showing that airflow is not limited. The value 1.25 inverts the fraction. The value 0.64 would come from a forced expiratory volume of 2.56 L, and 0.32 does not follow from these numbers.

cards.q: Predict the spirometry ratio in a patient with advanced emphysema.
cards.a: The ratio is reduced, because airflow is limited more than lung volume.
options: The ratio is raised, because elastic recoil is increased
The ratio is normal, because emphysema affects only gas exchange
The ratio is reduced, because airflow is limited more than lung volume
The ratio is reduced, because total lung capacity is decreased
cards.explanation: Emphysema destroys the elastic tissue that tethers small airways open, so they collapse during forced expiration and the first second delivers much less air than it should, dropping the ratio. Elastic recoil in emphysema is reduced, not increased. The disease clearly affects mechanics as well as exchange, and total lung capacity actually rises because of air trapping.

cards.q: Predict the spirometry ratio in a patient with pulmonary fibrosis.
cards.a: The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are reduced.
options: The ratio is reduced, while both measured volumes are reduced
The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are raised
The ratio is reduced, while both measured volumes are raised
The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are reduced
cards.explanation: Fibrosis shrinks the lung, so the forced expiratory volume in one second and the forced vital capacity both fall, but the stiff lung recoils hard and empties quickly, so the fraction delivered in the first second holds up or improves. A reduced ratio would indicate obstruction. Raised volumes do not occur in a lung that cannot expand normally.

cards.q: Why does airway obstruction lower the ratio rather than lowering both values equally?
cards.a: Narrowed airways slow the flow rate, so the first second is affected far more than the eventual total.
options: Narrowed airways slow the flow rate, so the first second is affected far more than the eventual total
Narrowed airways reduce total lung capacity, so the forced vital capacity falls first
Narrowed airways prevent full inspiration, so the maneuver cannot be completed
Narrowed airways also stiffen the surrounding lung tissue, so both measured values fall in equal proportion
cards.explanation: Given enough time an obstructed patient can still empty most of the lung, so the total exhaled volume is relatively preserved while the rate of emptying is not, which is exactly why the ratio is the diagnostic number. Obstruction does not primarily reduce lung size, and total lung capacity is often increased instead. Inspiration is generally easier than expiration in obstruction, and airway narrowing does not stiffen the parenchyma.

cards.q: Why does a restrictive process leave the ratio intact?
cards.a: Both the one second volume and the total capacity fall together, and strong recoil keeps flow rates high.
options: The forced vital capacity is unchanged in restriction, so only the one second volume falls and the ratio drops
Both the one second volume and the total capacity fall together, and strong recoil keeps flow rates high
Airway radius increases to compensate for the smaller lung
The measurement is taken over a longer interval in restrictive disease
cards.explanation: Restriction reduces the size of the lung without narrowing the airways, so the numerator and denominator shrink together and the stiff tissue actually pushes air out quickly, holding the ratio at or above normal. The forced vital capacity is definitely reduced in restriction rather than unchanged, so the numerator is not the only value that falls. Airway radius does not enlarge to compensate, and the one second interval is the same for every patient.

cards.q: Patient A has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 1.6 L and a forced vital capacity of 4.0 L. Classify the pattern and predict this patient's lung compliance and elastic recoil.
cards.a: Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil.
options: Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Obstructive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Restrictive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
cards.explanation: The ratio is 1.6 divided by 4.0, or 0.40, far below 0.70, so this is obstruction, and when the cause is emphysema the destroyed elastic tissue leaves a lung that inflates easily but recoils weakly. Restriction would show a preserved ratio with reduced volumes. Low compliance with high recoil is the fibrosis pairing, and it does not belong to an obstructive result of this kind.

cards.q: Patient B has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.1 L, a forced vital capacity of 2.5 L, and a total lung capacity of 4.0 L against a predicted 6.0 L. Classify the pattern and predict compliance and recoil.
cards.a: Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil.
options: Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Restrictive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Obstructive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
cards.explanation: The ratio is 2.1 divided by 2.5, which is 0.84, above normal, while the total lung capacity is only two thirds of predicted, so this is restriction, and a lung that cannot be filled is stiff, meaning low compliance and correspondingly strong recoil. An obstructive label would require a ratio below 0.70. High compliance with low recoil describes emphysema, the opposite mechanical picture.

cards.q: A spirometry report shows a forced vital capacity that is 60 percent of predicted and a ratio of 0.85. Working back from the result, what does this say about the lung?
cards.a: The lung is stiffer than normal and cannot be inflated to a normal size, but its airways are not narrowed.
options: The lung is stiffer than normal and cannot be inflated to a normal size, but its airways are not narrowed
The airways are narrowed and the lung tissue itself is normal
Both the airways and the lung tissue are normal, so the effort was poor
The lung is floppier than normal and traps air behind small airways that collapse during forced expiration
cards.explanation: A high ratio with a small capacity means air leaves quickly but there was not much to start with, which points to reduced expansion of stiff tissue rather than to any flow limitation. Narrowed airways would drag the ratio down instead of pushing it up. Poor effort tends to reduce both values without raising the ratio, and a floppy air trapping lung produces a low ratio with a raised total lung capacity.

cards.q: A patient with a baseline ratio of 0.55 inhales a bronchodilator, and the forced expiratory volume in one second rises by 18 percent while the forced vital capacity changes little. What does this response indicate about the obstruction?
cards.a: A large part of the obstruction is reversible airway smooth muscle contraction.
options: The obstruction is entirely due to permanent destruction of alveolar walls
A large part of the obstruction is reversible airway smooth muscle contraction
The result should be reclassified as a restrictive pattern
The lung tissue has become more compliant within minutes
cards.explanation: A bronchodilator acts on smooth muscle, so a marked jump in the one second volume shows that much of the narrowing was muscular tone rather than fixed structural change, which is characteristic of asthma. Destroyed alveolar walls cannot be reopened by a drug, so that would give little or no improvement. The ratio remains below normal, so the pattern is still obstructive, and tissue compliance does not change in minutes.

cards.q: How is minute ventilation calculated?
cards.a: Tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency.
options: Tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency
Tidal volume minus dead space, multiplied by breathing frequency
Vital capacity multiplied by breathing frequency
Tidal volume divided by breathing frequency
cards.explanation: Minute ventilation is simply all the air moved in and out per minute, so it is the size of each breath times how many breaths occur. Subtracting dead space first gives alveolar ventilation, a smaller and more meaningful number. Vital capacity is a maximal effort rather than a resting breath, and dividing would not give a volume per minute.

cards.q: How is alveolar ventilation calculated?
cards.a: Tidal volume minus dead space volume, multiplied by breathing frequency.
options: Tidal volume multiplied by the breathing frequency in breaths per minute
Tidal volume minus dead space volume, multiplied by breathing frequency
Minute ventilation multiplied by dead space volume
Dead space volume multiplied by breathing frequency
cards.explanation: Only the part of each breath that gets past the conducting airways can exchange gas, so dead space must be subtracted from every breath before multiplying by rate. Tidal volume times frequency gives minute ventilation, which overstates useful ventilation. Dead space times frequency gives dead space ventilation, the wasted portion.

cards.q: What is the approximate anatomic dead space volume in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 150 mL.
options: About 350 mL
About 500 mL
About 150 mL
About 50 mL
cards.explanation: The conducting airways hold roughly 150 mL, so a 500 mL breath delivers only about 350 mL of fresh air to the alveoli. The 350 mL figure is that useful portion rather than the dead space itself. About 500 mL is the whole tidal volume, and 50 mL is far too small for the entire airway tree.

cards.q: What is anatomic dead space?
cards.a: The volume of the conducting airways, where no gas exchange occurs.
options: The volume of alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
The volume of air left in the lung after maximal expiration
The volume of alveoli that are perfused but not ventilated
The volume of the conducting airways, where no gas exchange occurs
cards.explanation: Anatomic dead space is a structural volume, the air sitting in the nose, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles where there is no exchange surface. Ventilated but unperfused alveoli make up alveolar dead space, a functional rather than anatomic category. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume, and perfused but unventilated alveoli form a shunt.

cards.q: What is alveolar dead space?
cards.a: Alveoli that receive air but receive little or no blood flow.
options: Alveoli that receive air but receive little or no blood flow
Alveoli that receive blood but receive no air
The air in the trachea and bronchi at the end of a breath
Alveoli that have collapsed and hold no air
cards.explanation: An alveolus with air but no capillary blood flow cannot exchange anything, so its ventilation is wasted just as thoroughly as air sitting in the trachea. Alveoli with blood but no air are a shunt, the opposite mismatch. Air in the trachea and bronchi is anatomic dead space, and collapsed alveoli are atelectatic rather than dead space.

cards.q: What is physiologic dead space?
cards.a: Anatomic dead space plus alveolar dead space.
options: Anatomic dead space minus alveolar dead space
Anatomic dead space plus alveolar dead space
Alveolar dead space minus anatomic dead space
Tidal volume minus anatomic dead space
cards.explanation: Physiologic dead space is the total wasted ventilation from both sources, and in a healthy person it is nearly equal to the anatomic dead space because alveolar dead space is very small. The subtractions do not describe any real quantity. Tidal volume minus anatomic dead space is the useful fresh air per breath, the opposite of wasted volume.

cards.q: What is a typical resting breathing frequency for a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 12 breaths per minute.
options: About 4 breaths per minute
About 12 breaths per minute
About 30 breaths per minute
About 60 breaths per minute
cards.explanation: Twelve breaths of about 500 mL give the familiar resting minute ventilation of 6 L/min. Four breaths per minute would be severe hypoventilation. Thirty breaths per minute is the rapid shallow pattern of distress, and 60 is a newborn rate rather than an adult one.

cards.q: Which measure best predicts how well the blood is oxygenated and cleared of carbon dioxide?
cards.a: Alveolar ventilation.
options: Minute ventilation
Tidal volume alone
Alveolar ventilation
Breathing frequency alone
cards.explanation: Only air that reaches exchange surface can change blood gases, so alveolar ventilation is the number that tracks arterial PCO2. Minute ventilation can look completely normal while alveolar ventilation is dangerously low. Tidal volume and frequency each tell only half the story, since the same minute ventilation can come from very different combinations.

cards.q: A person breathes 500 mL fourteen times per minute. What is the minute ventilation?
cards.a: 7000 mL/min.
options: 514 mL/min
4900 mL/min
6000 mL/min
7000 mL/min
cards.explanation: Minute ventilation is 500 times 14, which is 7000 mL/min or 7 L/min. Adding the two numbers gives 514, which is not a rate. The value 4900 would be the alveolar ventilation once a 150 mL dead space is subtracted, and 6000 corresponds to twelve breaths rather than fourteen.

cards.q: A person breathes 500 mL twelve times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
cards.a: 4200 mL/min.
options: 4200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
1800 mL/min
5850 mL/min
cards.explanation: Each breath delivers 500 minus 150, or 350 mL, and twelve of those give 4200 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, which ignores dead space. The value 1800 is the dead space ventilation, and 5850 comes from subtracting the dead space only once instead of from every breath.

cards.q: A patient breathes 400 mL fifteen times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
cards.a: 3750 mL/min.
options: 6000 mL/min
3750 mL/min
2250 mL/min
5850 mL/min
cards.explanation: Fresh air per breath is 400 minus 150, or 250 mL, and multiplying by 15 gives 3750 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation before dead space is removed. The value 2250 is dead space ventilation, and 5850 subtracts the dead space only once from the whole minute.

cards.q: A patient has a minute ventilation of 6 L/min at a rate of 12 breaths per minute. What is the tidal volume?
options: 72 mL
350 mL
500 mL
720 mL
cards.explanation: Rearranging minute ventilation as tidal volume times frequency gives 6000 divided by 12, which is 500 mL. The value 72 comes from dividing the wrong way. The value 350 is the fresh air per breath after a 150 mL dead space is subtracted, not the tidal volume itself.

cards.q: A patient breathes 300 mL twenty times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
cards.a: 3000 mL/min.
options: 6000 mL/min
4500 mL/min
3000 mL/min
1500 mL/min
cards.explanation: Only 150 mL of each 300 mL breath gets past the dead space, and 150 times 20 gives 3000 mL/min, half of the alveolar ventilation a normal pattern would provide at the same minute ventilation. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation. The other values do not follow from this tidal volume and rate.

cards.q: A patient breathes 750 mL eight times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
cards.a: 4800 mL/min.
options: 1200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
5850 mL/min
4800 mL/min
cards.explanation: Fresh air per breath is 750 minus 150, or 600 mL, and 600 times 8 gives 4800 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, and 1200 is the dead space ventilation. The value 5850 wrongly subtracts a single 150 mL from the minute total instead of from each breath.

cards.q: A swimmer breathes through a snorkel that adds 200 mL of dead space, breathing 500 mL twelve times per minute. What is the alveolar ventilation?
cards.a: 1800 mL/min.
options: 1800 mL/min
4200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
3600 mL/min
cards.explanation: Total dead space becomes 150 plus 200, or 350 mL, so each breath delivers only 150 mL and twelve breaths give 1800 mL/min, far below the normal 4200. The value 4200 ignores the added tubing. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, which the snorkel does not change at all, which is exactly why minute ventilation is a misleading number here.

cards.q: Person A breathes 1000 mL six times per minute and Person B breathes 250 mL twenty four times per minute. Dead space is 150 mL in both. Compare their minute and alveolar ventilations.
cards.a: Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 5100 mL/min in A and 2400 mL/min in B.
options: Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 5100 mL/min in A and 2400 mL/min in B
Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, and alveolar ventilation is also equal in both
Minute ventilation is higher in B, and alveolar ventilation is also higher in B
Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 2400 mL/min in A and 5100 mL/min in B
cards.explanation: Both move 6 L/min, but A wastes 150 mL only six times while B wastes it twenty four times, so A delivers 850 times 6 equals 5100 mL/min and B delivers 100 times 24 equals 2400 mL/min. Equal alveolar ventilations would require equal dead space fractions, which deep and shallow breathing do not have. Minute ventilation is identical rather than higher in B, and reversing the two values contradicts the arithmetic.

cards.q: A patient in distress breathes 200 mL thirty times per minute with a 150 mL dead space. Calculate alveolar ventilation and predict arterial PCO2.
cards.a: Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 rises.
options: Alveolar ventilation is 6000 mL/min and arterial PCO2 falls
Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 falls
Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 rises
Alveolar ventilation is 4500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 stays normal
cards.explanation: Only 50 mL of each breath clears the dead space, so 50 times 30 gives 1500 mL/min, roughly a third of normal, and since carbon dioxide removal depends on alveolar ventilation, PCO2 climbs even though minute ventilation is a normal looking 6000 mL/min. Reporting 6000 as alveolar ventilation confuses the two measures. Falling PCO2 would require hyperventilation at the alveolar level, which is the opposite of what is happening here.

cards.q: A clot blocks blood flow to a region of lung while that region keeps receiving air. Predict the effect on physiologic dead space and on alveolar ventilation at unchanged minute ventilation.
cards.a: Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation falls.
options: Physiologic dead space falls and effective alveolar ventilation rises
Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation falls
Physiologic dead space is unchanged because the airways are normal
Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation rises to compensate
cards.explanation: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused add alveolar dead space to the anatomic dead space, so more of every breath is wasted and less of the same minute ventilation actually exchanges gas. Dead space cannot fall when a perfusion defect appears. Physiologic dead space includes both anatomic and alveolar components, so normal airways do not keep it unchanged, and effective alveolar ventilation cannot rise while the wasted fraction grows.

cards.q: A patient has a minute ventilation of 8 L/min at 32 breaths per minute, yet arterial PCO2 is rising. Dead space is 150 mL. Work out why.
cards.a: Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 3200 mL/min despite the high minute ventilation.
options: Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 3200 mL/min despite the high minute ventilation
Tidal volume is 500 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 11200 mL/min and the rise must come from another cause
Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 8000 mL/min and dead space is irrelevant
Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 4800 mL/min, which is normal
cards.explanation: Dividing 8000 by 32 gives a tidal volume of 250 mL, and subtracting the 150 mL dead space leaves 100 mL per breath, so alveolar ventilation is 100 times 32, or 3200 mL/min, well below the normal 4200. A tidal volume of 500 mL would require a minute ventilation of 16 L/min at this rate. Alveolar ventilation can never equal minute ventilation while dead space exists, and 4800 does not match the arithmetic.

cards.q: What does a spirometer record?
cards.a: The volume of air moved into and out of the lungs over time.
options: The volume of air moved into and out of the lungs over time
The pressure inside the pleural cavity during each breath
The percentage of oxygen in the exhaled air
The rate of blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries
cards.explanation: A spirometer measures moving volume against time, which is why every value it reports is either a volume or a flow derived from one. Pleural pressure requires an esophageal balloon or a direct measurement, not a mouthpiece. Exhaled gas fractions come from a gas analyzer, and pulmonary blood flow is not measured by this instrument at all.

cards.q: What do the two axes of a standard spirogram show?
cards.a: Volume on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis.
options: Pressure on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis
Volume on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis
Flow on the vertical axis and pressure on the horizontal axis
Time on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis
cards.explanation: Reading volume against time lets you see both how much air moved and how quickly, which is what makes the one second measurement possible. A pressure volume plot is used to study compliance, not to record a breathing trace. Flow against volume gives the flow volume loop, a different display, and swapping the axes is simply not the convention.

cards.q: Which value cannot be obtained from a spirogram alone?
cards.a: Residual volume.
options: Vital capacity
Tidal volume
Residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume
cards.explanation: The spirometer only sees air that passes the mouthpiece, and residual volume never leaves the lung, so it and every capacity containing it must be measured by another method. Vital capacity, tidal volume, and expiratory reserve volume are all exhaled through the instrument and are read directly from the trace.

cards.q: Which capacities can be calculated directly from a spirogram?
cards.a: Vital capacity and inspiratory capacity.
options: Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity
Total lung capacity and vital capacity
Functional residual capacity and inspiratory capacity
Vital capacity and inspiratory capacity
cards.explanation: Both of these are built only from volumes that move through the mouthpiece, so they can be read straight off the trace. Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity each contain residual volume, which the spirometer cannot see, so neither can be obtained without a dilution or plethysmography technique.

cards.q: Which subject characteristics are used to calculate predicted lung volumes?
cards.a: Height, age, and sex.
options: Height, age, and sex
Blood pressure, pulse, and body temperature
Resting breathing rate and tidal volume
Hemoglobin concentration and arterial PO2
cards.explanation: Lung size scales with body size and declines with age, and reference equations use height, age, and sex to give the value a healthy person of that description should reach. Vital signs describe cardiovascular state rather than lung size. Breathing pattern is a result rather than a predictor, and blood measurements report gas transport rather than lung volume.

cards.q: How is percent predicted calculated for a lung volume?
cards.a: Measured value divided by predicted value, multiplied by 100.
options: Predicted value divided by measured value, multiplied by 100
Measured value divided by predicted value, multiplied by 100
Measured value minus predicted value, divided by 100
Measured value plus predicted value, divided by 2
cards.explanation: Percent predicted expresses the measured result as a fraction of what was expected, so the measured value goes on top and the result is a straightforward percentage. Inverting the fraction would make a small lung look large. Subtracting gives a raw difference in liters rather than a percentage, and averaging the two numbers has no interpretive meaning.

cards.q: Why is a nose clip used during spirometry?
cards.a: To prevent air escaping through the nose instead of the mouthpiece.
options: To slow the rate of breathing during the maneuver
To prevent the subject from smelling the equipment
To prevent air escaping through the nose instead of the mouthpiece
To keep the upper airway humidified during a forced expiratory maneuver
cards.explanation: The spirometer can only measure what goes through it, so any air lost through the nose makes every recorded volume too small. The clip does not change breathing rate, which the subject controls. Smell is irrelevant to the measurement, and humidification of the upper airway happens regardless of the clip.

cards.q: Which maneuver measures vital capacity?
cards.a: A maximal inspiration followed immediately by a maximal expiration.
options: A single quiet breath in and out
A maximal inspiration held for ten seconds
A maximal expiration followed by a period of quiet tidal breathing
A maximal inspiration followed immediately by a maximal expiration
cards.explanation: Vital capacity is the largest volume a person can move voluntarily, so the lung must be filled completely and then emptied completely in one continuous effort. A quiet breath gives only the tidal volume. Holding a breath records no volume change, and a maximal expiration alone leaves out the inspiratory half of the excursion.

cards.q: A student measures a vital capacity of 3.6 L against a predicted value of 4.5 L. What is the percent predicted?
cards.a: 80 percent.
options: 80 percent
125 percent
90 percent
20 percent
cards.explanation: Dividing 3.6 by 4.5 gives 0.80, so the student reached 80 percent of the predicted value. Inverting the fraction gives 125 percent and would suggest a larger than expected lung. The value 20 percent is the shortfall rather than the result, and 90 percent does not follow from these numbers.

cards.q: A student measures a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.0 L against a predicted 3.2 L. What is the percent predicted?
cards.a: 62.5 percent.
options: 160 percent
62.5 percent
37.5 percent
64 percent
cards.explanation: Dividing 2.0 by 3.2 gives 0.625, so the measured value is 62.5 percent of predicted. The value 160 percent comes from inverting the fraction. The value 37.5 percent is the shortfall from predicted rather than the percent achieved, and 64 percent does not match the division.

cards.q: A lab group needs to determine total lung capacity, but the spirometer cannot supply it. Which approach is required?
cards.a: A helium dilution or nitrogen washout test to find residual volume first.
options: Repeating the vital capacity maneuver with greater effort
Adding the tidal volume to the vital capacity
A helium dilution or nitrogen washout test to find residual volume first
Measuring the forced expiratory volume in one second and doubling it
cards.explanation: Total lung capacity contains residual volume, so the missing piece must be found by a method that measures gas still inside the lung, and then it is added to the vital capacity. Greater effort cannot expel air that is trapped by definition. Adding tidal volume double counts, since it is already inside vital capacity, and doubling a one second volume has no physiological basis.

cards.q: On a recorded spirogram, from which point does the expiratory reserve volume excursion begin?
cards.a: From the resting level at the end of a quiet expiration.
options: From the peak of a maximal inspiration
From the lowest point of a maximal expiration
From the peak of a quiet inspiration
From the resting level at the end of a quiet expiration
cards.explanation: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be forced out after an ordinary breath has already been let go, so the trace must start at the resting end expiratory level and go down from there. Starting at maximal inspiration would trace the vital capacity instead. The lowest point of the trace is the end of that excursion, and starting from a quiet inspiration would include the tidal volume.

cards.q: A student stops exhaling early during the vital capacity maneuver. What is the effect on the recorded value?
cards.a: Vital capacity is underestimated.
options: Vital capacity is underestimated
Vital capacity is overestimated
Vital capacity is unaffected because the maneuver is standardized
Vital capacity is unaffected but residual volume appears larger
cards.explanation: The instrument records only the air that actually passed the mouthpiece, so stopping short leaves part of the expiratory reserve volume in the lung and the number comes out too small. It cannot be overestimated, since no extra air was moved. Standardizing the instructions does not guarantee full effort, and residual volume is not recorded by a spirometer in the first place.

cards.q: Two healthy students of the same age and sex are tested, one 150 cm tall and one 190 cm tall. How should their predicted vital capacities compare?
cards.a: The taller student has the larger predicted vital capacity.
options: The shorter student has the larger predicted vital capacity
The taller student has the larger predicted vital capacity
Both have the same predicted vital capacity, since age and sex match
Predicted values cannot be compared between two people
cards.explanation: Reference equations scale strongly with height because a taller thorax houses larger lungs, so the 190 cm student is expected to move considerably more air. The relationship runs with height rather than against it. Age and sex are only two of the three inputs, and comparing predicted values across subjects is exactly what reference equations are for.

cards.q: A student records a vital capacity that is 105 percent of predicted. How should this result be interpreted?
cards.a: As a normal result, since predicted values describe an average rather than a ceiling.
options: As evidence of emphysema, since the lung is holding more air than the reference equation expects
As a measurement error, since values above 100 percent are impossible
As a normal result, since predicted values describe an average rather than a ceiling
As evidence of restriction, since the value differs from predicted
cards.explanation: Predicted equations give the center of a healthy range, so results modestly above or below 100 percent are ordinary, and roughly 80 to 120 percent is generally treated as normal. Emphysema raises total lung capacity through trapping but lowers vital capacity. Values above predicted are entirely possible, and restriction would show a value well below predicted rather than above it.

cards.q: From a spirogram a student reads a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 2900 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1300 mL, with a predicted vital capacity of 5000 mL. Calculate the vital capacity and the percent predicted.
cards.a: Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 94 percent of predicted.
options: Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 94 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 106 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 3400 mL, which is 68 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 4200 mL, which is 84 percent of predicted
cards.explanation: Adding 500 plus 2900 plus 1300 gives 4700 mL, and 4700 divided by 5000 is 0.94, a normal result. The figure 106 percent comes from inverting the fraction. A vital capacity of 3400 leaves out the inspiratory reserve or the tidal volume, and 4200 omits the tidal volume from the sum.

cards.q: A student records a vital capacity of 3.2 L against a predicted 4.6 L, with a ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity of 0.85. Interpret the pair of findings.
cards.a: A restrictive pattern, since volume is markedly reduced while airflow is well preserved.
options: An obstructive pattern, since the measured vital capacity is well below the predicted value
A restrictive pattern, since volume is markedly reduced while airflow is well preserved
A normal result, since the ratio is above 0.80
An obstructive pattern, since the ratio is above 0.80
cards.explanation: The measured vital capacity is about 70 percent of predicted, which is a real reduction, yet the high ratio shows air is leaving quickly, and that combination defines restriction. A reduced volume by itself does not indicate obstruction, which is defined by a low ratio. Calling the result normal ignores how far the volume falls short, and a high ratio is the opposite of the obstructive finding.

cards.q: A student records a vital capacity of 4.6 L against a predicted 4.7 L, but a ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity of 0.62. Interpret the pair of findings.
cards.a: An obstructive pattern, since airflow is limited even though lung volume is normal.
options: A normal result, since the vital capacity is 98 percent of predicted
A restrictive pattern, since the ratio is below 0.70
An obstructive pattern, since airflow is limited even though lung volume is normal
A measurement error, since a normal lung volume cannot occur together with a low ratio
cards.explanation: Obstruction is defined by how fast air leaves, not by how much the lung holds, so a normal capacity with a ratio of 0.62 is exactly the early obstructive picture seen in asthma. A normal volume alone does not clear the result, since the ratio is the diagnostic number. A low ratio never indicates restriction, and this combination is common in practice rather than impossible.

cards.q: Two students of identical height obtain very different results, and the one with the lower values had a poor seal around the mouthpiece. Predict how the leak affected the recorded volumes and the calculated percent predicted.
cards.a: All recorded volumes are too low, so every percent predicted value is falsely reduced.
options: All recorded volumes are too high, so every percent predicted value is falsely raised
Only the forced expiratory volume in one second is affected, so the ratio falls
All recorded volumes are too low, so every percent predicted value is falsely reduced
The volumes are unaffected because the predicted values correct for technique
cards.explanation: Air escaping around the lips never reaches the sensor, so every volume the instrument sees is smaller than the volume the lung actually moved, and dividing those small numbers by unchanged predicted values makes the student look falsely restricted. A leak cannot add volume to the record. It affects both the one second volume and the total similarly rather than only one, and predicted equations depend on body size and cannot correct for a technical fault.
